title: A Roman Family
author: Stemma
intro: Meet a Roman family: father Lucius, mother Cornelia, their children Marcus and Julia, and the household slave Davus. Everything is in the present tense, with the simplest nouns of the 1st and 2nd declensions, so you can watch the endings at work.

tr.en: Here is a Roman family.
tr.it: Ecco una famiglia romana.
tr.es: He aquí una familia romana.

tr.en: The family lives in a large country house near Rome.
tr.it: La famiglia abita in una grande villa vicino a Roma.
tr.es: La familia vive en una gran villa cerca de Roma.

tr.en: Lucius is the father, Cornelia is the mother.
tr.it: Lucio è il padre, Cornelia è la madre.
tr.es: Lucio es el padre, Cornelia es la madre.

tr.en: Marcus is the son, Julia is the daughter.
tr.it: Marco è il figlio, Giulia è la figlia.
tr.es: Marco es el hijo, Julia es la hija.

tr.en: Marcus is a little boy, Julia is a cheerful girl.
tr.it: Marco è un bambino piccolo, Giulia è una ragazza allegra.
tr.es: Marco es un niño pequeño, Julia es una niña alegre.

tr.en: Davus is a slave; he works in the house.
tr.it: Davo è uno schiavo; lavora nella villa.
tr.es: Davo es un esclavo; trabaja en la villa.

tr.en: Father is walking in the garden, mother is sitting in the atrium.
tr.it: Il padre passeggia nel giardino, la madre siede nell'atrio.
tr.es: El padre pasea por el jardín, la madre está sentada en el atrio.

tr.en: Mother calls her daughter: “Julia, where are you?”
tr.it: La madre chiama la figlia: «Giulia, dove sei?»
tr.es: La madre llama a su hija: «Julia, ¿dónde estás?»

tr.en: “Here I am, mother!” Julia answers.
tr.it: «Sono qui, mamma!» risponde Giulia.
tr.es: «¡Aquí estoy, madre!», responde Julia.

tr.en: Marcus is not working, but playing in the garden.
tr.it: Marco non lavora, ma gioca nel giardino.
tr.es: Marco no trabaja, sino que juega en el jardín.

tr.en: Davus carries water and prepares dinner.
tr.it: Davo porta l'acqua e prepara la cena.
tr.es: Davo lleva agua y prepara la cena.

tr.en: In the evening the whole family dines in the dining room.
tr.it: La sera tutta la famiglia cena nel triclinio.
tr.es: Por la tarde toda la familia cena en el triclinio.

tr.en: The Roman family is happy.
tr.it: La famiglia romana è felice.
tr.es: La familia romana es feliz.

notes.n: ecce 'look! here is…' points at something; it survives in Italian ecco.
A vīlla was a country house with its farm. It gave Italian villa, but also French ville 'town' and English village.
Latin has no articles: pater means 'father', 'the father' or 'a father'. The Romance articles grew out of ille 'that': Italian il, Spanish el, French le.
fīlius, fīlia → Italian figlio, figlia; Spanish hijo, hija (Latin f- became h- in Spanish); French fils, fille; Portuguese filho, filha; Romanian fiu, fiică.
servus → Italian servo, English serve, servant. labōrāre 'to toil' → Italian lavorare 'to work', Spanish labrar 'to till', French labourer 'to plough'.
hortus 'garden' → Italian orto, Spanish huerto 'vegetable garden'. The ātrium was the central hall of a Roman house, with an opening to the sky in the middle of its roof.
Iūlia here is vocative, the case for calling someone; in the 1st declension it looks the same as the nominative.
The verb ending shows the person: labōrat 'he works', lūdit 'he plays'. Latin needs no subject pronoun, just like Italian lavora and Spanish trabaja.
vesperī 'in the evening' is an old locative of vesper (→ Italian vespro 'vespers', Spanish víspera 'eve'). cēna 'dinner' → Italian cena, Spanish cena, Romanian cină.

title: At School
author: Stemma
intro: Marcus goes to school. Roman children of well-off families learnt literature with a grammaticus, often a Greek, who had them read aloud and explain the poets, above all Homer and Vergil. A slave called the paedagogus walked the child to school and carried his things.

tr.en: In the morning Marcus walks to school.
tr.it: Al mattino Marco va a scuola a piedi.
tr.es: Por la mañana Marco va a pie a la escuela.

tr.en: The paedagogus, a Greek slave, carries his books and writing tablets.
tr.it: Il pedagogo, uno schiavo greco, porta i libri e le tavolette.
tr.es: El pedagogo, un esclavo griego, lleva los libros y las tablillas.

tr.en: In the school sit many boys and a few girls.
tr.it: A scuola siedono molti ragazzi e poche ragazze.
tr.es: En la escuela se sientan muchos chicos y pocas chicas.

tr.en: The teacher is Theodorus, a Greek grammaticus.
tr.it: Il maestro è Teodoro, un grammatico greco.
tr.es: El maestro es Teodoro, un gramático griego.

tr.en: Theodorus opens a book and recites the words of Vergil.
tr.it: Teodoro apre un libro e recita le parole di Virgilio.
tr.es: Teodoro abre un libro y recita las palabras de Virgilio.

tr.en: The boys and girls are silent and listen.
tr.it: Ragazzi e ragazze tacciono e ascoltano.
tr.es: Los chicos y las chicas callan y escuchan.

tr.en: Then the teacher asks: “Who is Aeneas?”
tr.it: Poi il grammatico chiede: «Chi è Enea?»
tr.es: Entonces el gramático pregunta: «¿Quién es Eneas?»

tr.en: Marcus answers: “Aeneas is a man from Troy.”
tr.it: Marco risponde: «Enea è un uomo di Troia.»
tr.es: Marco responde: «Eneas es un hombre de Troya.»

tr.en: “Well done, Marcus!” says the teacher.
tr.it: «Bene, Marco!» dice il grammatico.
tr.es: «¡Bien, Marco!», dice el gramático.

tr.en: But Sextus is not listening: he is drawing a horse on his tablet.
tr.it: Ma Sesto non ascolta: disegna un cavallo sulla tavoletta.
tr.es: Pero Sexto no escucha: dibuja un caballo en su tablilla.

tr.en: The teacher is angry and shouts: “Sextus, why aren't you listening?”
tr.it: Il grammatico è arrabbiato e grida: «Sesto, perché non ascolti?»
tr.es: El gramático está enfadado y grita: «Sexto, ¿por qué no escuchas?»

tr.en: Sextus is afraid and says nothing; the boys laugh.
tr.it: Sesto ha paura e tace; i ragazzi ridono.
tr.es: Sexto tiene miedo y calla; los chicos se ríen.

tr.en: At noon the boys and girls run home happily.
tr.it: A mezzogiorno ragazzi e ragazze corrono a casa contenti.
tr.es: A mediodía los chicos y las chicas corren a casa contentos.

notes.n: māne 'in the morning': from dē māne come Italian domani and French demain 'tomorrow'; Romanian mâine 'tomorrow' continues māne itself, and Spanish mañana comes from a related form *maneāna.

The paedagōgus (Greek 'child-leader') was the slave who took a boy to school and watched over him: English pedagogue. tabella, a small wax tablet, is a diminutive of tabula 'board' (→ Italian tavola, Spanish tabla).
The grammaticus taught children of about 11 to 15 to read and explain the poets, Greek and Latin; younger children learnt letters and sums from a lūdī magister.
aperīre 'to open' → Italian aprire, Spanish abrir, French ouvrir. Vergiliī is genitive: 'of Vergil'. verbum 'word' → Spanish verbo, English verb; French verve.
Quis? 'who?'. The Romance words come from related forms: Spanish quién from quem, Italian chi from quī.
bene 'well' → Italian bene, Spanish and French bien, Portuguese bem, Romanian bine. inquit 'says' is only used inside or right after a quotation.

Sextus was a common Roman first name, literally 'sixth' (sextus); Quīntus 'fifth' and Decimus 'tenth' are names of the same kind. equus 'horse' was replaced in everyday speech by caballus 'nag' (Italian cavallo, Spanish caballo, French cheval), but the feminine equa lives on in Spanish yegua, Portuguese égua and Romanian iapă 'mare'.
Sexte is the vocative of Sextus, like Mārce from Mārcus.
timēre 'to fear' → Italian temere, Spanish temer; tacēre 'to be silent' → Italian tacere, English tacit.
merīdiēs 'midday' (from medius diēs) also meant 'south': English meridian, and a.m./p.m. = ante/post merīdiem. A mixed group (puerī et puellae) takes a masculine plural adjective: laetī.

title: At the Market
author: Stemma
intro: Cornelia and Julia go shopping in the forum, the bustling heart of a Roman town, where temples, shops and market stalls stood side by side. Watch for the vocative (Mārce!) and two useful phrases for asking and giving a price.

tr.en: Today Cornelia and Julia walk to the forum.
tr.it: Oggi Cornelia e Giulia vanno a piedi al foro.
tr.es: Hoy Cornelia y Julia van caminando al foro.

tr.en: Davus is there too, and he carries a big basket.
tr.it: C'è anche Davo, e porta una grande cesta.
tr.es: También está Davo, y lleva una gran cesta.

tr.en: In the forum many Romans walk about and shout.
tr.it: Nel foro molti Romani passeggiano e gridano.
tr.es: En el foro muchos romanos pasean y gritan.

tr.en: There are temples, shops and statues there.
tr.it: Lì ci sono templi, botteghe e statue.
tr.es: Allí hay templos, tiendas y estatuas.

tr.en: A farmer is selling grapes and apples in the forum.
tr.it: Un contadino vende uva e mele nel foro.
tr.es: Un campesino vende uvas y manzanas en el foro.

tr.en: “Look, good grapes!” shouts the farmer.
tr.it: «Ecco dell'uva buona!» grida il contadino.
tr.es: «¡Mirad, uvas buenas!», grita el campesino.

tr.en: Julia looks at the grapes and asks: “How much are the grapes?”
tr.it: Giulia guarda l'uva e chiede: «Quanto costa l'uva?»
tr.es: Julia mira las uvas y pregunta: «¿Cuánto cuestan las uvas?»

tr.en: “Two sesterces,” the farmer answers.
tr.it: «Due sesterzi», risponde il contadino.
tr.es: «Dos sestercios», responde el campesino.

tr.en: Cornelia hands over the money, and Davus puts the grapes into the basket.
tr.it: Cornelia dà il denaro e Davo mette l'uva nella cesta.
tr.es: Cornelia da el dinero y Davo pone las uvas en la cesta.

tr.en: Suddenly Julia sees Marcus.
tr.it: All'improvviso Giulia vede Marco.
tr.es: De repente Julia ve a Marco.

tr.en: Marcus is playing with his friends near a temple.
tr.it: Marco gioca con gli amici vicino a un tempio.
tr.es: Marco juega con sus amigos cerca de un templo.

tr.en: “Marcus, why are you in the forum?” asks his mother.
tr.it: «Marco, perché sei nel foro?» chiede la madre.
tr.es: «Marco, ¿por qué estás en el foro?», pregunta su madre.

tr.en: “The teacher is ill!” Marcus answers, and laughs.
tr.it: «Il maestro è malato!» risponde Marco, e ride.
tr.es: «¡El maestro está enfermo!», responde Marco, y se ríe.

tr.en: Then Cornelia and the children walk home with Davus.
tr.it: Poi Cornelia e i bambini tornano a casa a piedi con Davo.
tr.es: Luego Cornelia y los niños vuelven a casa a pie con Davo.

notes.n: ad forum: ad + accusative means motion towards. The forum was a town's main square: market, law courts and temples in one place.
adest 'is present' is ad + est. sporta 'basket' survives in Italian sporta 'shopping bag'.
taberna 'shop, stall, inn' → Italian taverna, Spanish taberna, English tavern.

agricola 'farmer' is masculine although it belongs to the 1st declension, like nauta 'sailor'. mālum 'apple' (long ā) is a different word from malum 'evil' (short a). Romanian măr 'apple' continues mālum; Spanish manzana and Portuguese maçã come from (māla) Matiāna, a variety of apple.
Quantī? 'at how much?' is a genitive of price.
duōbus sēstertiīs 'for two sesterces' is an ablative of price. The sēstertius was the usual coin for everyday prices.
subitō 'suddenly' → Italian subito, which now means 'at once'.
Mārce is the vocative of Mārcus: 2nd-declension nouns in -us end in -e when you address someone.
magister 'master, teacher' → Italian maestro, Spanish maestro, French maître, English master. aegrōtāre 'to be ill' comes from aeger 'sick'.
līberī 'children' literally means 'the free ones', the free-born members of the household. domum 'homewards' needs no preposition, like Rōmam 'to Rome'.

title: Famous Sayings
author: Various
source: Terence, Caesar, Vergil, Horace, Seneca, Juvenal, Pliny, Vegetius, medieval mottos, Descartes
intro: Nineteen famous Latin sayings, from the comic poet Terence to the philosopher Descartes. Many are still quoted every day; each note names the author or source. Short as they are, they show imperatives, perfects and the free word order of Latin.

tr.en: Seize the day.
tr.it: Cogli l'attimo.
tr.es: Aprovecha el día.

tr.en: I came, I saw, I conquered.
tr.it: Venni, vidi, vinsi.
tr.es: Vine, vi, vencí.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. f.

tr.en: The die is cast.
tr.it: Il dado è tratto.
tr.es: La suerte está echada.

tr.en: To err is human.
tr.it: Errare è umano.
tr.es: Errar es humano.

tr.en: Make haste slowly.
tr.it: Affrettati lentamente.
tr.es: Apresúrate despacio.

tr.en: Through hardships to the stars.
tr.it: Attraverso le asperità fino alle stelle.
tr.es: A través de las dificultades hasta las estrellas.

tr.en: A healthy mind in a healthy body.
tr.it: Mente sana in corpo sano.
tr.es: Mente sana en cuerpo sano.

tr.en: While I breathe, I hope.
tr.it: Finché respiro, spero.
tr.es: Mientras respiro, espero.

tr.en: I think, therefore I am.
tr.it: Penso, dunque sono.
tr.es: Pienso, luego existo.

tr.en: Pray and work.
tr.it: Prega e lavora.
tr.es: Reza y trabaja.

tr.en: Time flies.
tr.it: Il tempo fugge.
tr.es: El tiempo vuela.

tr.en: Remember that you must die.
tr.it: Ricordati che devi morire.
tr.es: Recuerda que has de morir.

tr.en: In wine there is truth.
tr.it: Nel vino c'è la verità.
tr.es: En el vino está la verdad.

tr.en: Fortune helps the brave.
tr.it: La fortuna aiuta gli audaci.
tr.es: La fortuna ayuda a los valientes.

tr.en: If you want peace, prepare for war.
tr.it: Se vuoi la pace, prepara la guerra.
tr.es: Si quieres la paz, prepara la guerra.

tr.en: Art is long, life is short.
tr.it: L'arte è lunga, la vita è breve.
tr.es: El arte es largo, la vida es breve.

tr.en: Love conquers all.
tr.it: L'amore vince tutto.
tr.es: El amor todo lo vence.

tr.en: People learn while they teach.
tr.it: Gli uomini, mentre insegnano, imparano.
tr.es: Los hombres, mientras enseñan, aprenden.

tr.en: No day without a line.
tr.it: Nessun giorno senza una linea.
tr.es: Ningún día sin una línea.

notes.n: Horace, Odes 1.11.8 (23 BC): carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō, 'seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow'. carpere means 'to pluck' fruit or flowers.

Julius Caesar's summary of his lightning victory over Pharnaces at Zela in 47 BC: Suetonius (Divus Iulius 37) says the words were carried on a placard in his Pontic triumph; Plutarch (Caesar 50) has him write them to a friend in Rome. Three perfects with long stem vowels: veniō → vēnī, videō → vīdī, vincō → vīcī.

Caesar, crossing the Rubicon into Italy with his army in 49 BC (Suetonius, Divus Iulius 32, has iacta ālea est; Plutarch says he spoke the words in Greek). iacta est is a perfect passive: participle + sum.
A proverb with ancient roots: Cicero (Philippics 12.5) says any man can err, but only a fool persists in error. An infinitive used as a subject takes a neuter adjective: hūmānum.

The favourite saying of the emperor Augustus, who said it in Greek, speûde bradéōs (Suetonius, Augustus 25). Italian lentamente is lentā mente 'with a slow mind': the Romance adverb ending -mente/-ment comes from the ablative of mēns.

A motto, used by many schools and air forces; compare Seneca, Hercules Furens 437: nōn est ad astra mollis ē terrīs via, 'there is no easy way from the earth to the stars'. astrum 'star' → Italian astro.
Juvenal, Satires 10.356 (early 2nd c. AD): one should pray for a sound mind in a sound body. mēns → Italian, Spanish mente; corpus → Italian corpo, Spanish cuerpo, French corps.

A motto (for example of the state of South Carolina); Cicero (Ad Atticum 9.10.3) quotes the saying that while there is life there is hope. spīrāre 'breathe' → Italian respirare, English spirit; spērāre → Italian sperare, Spanish esperar, French espérer.

René Descartes, Principia philosophiae 1.7 (1644); he had first written it in French: je pense, donc je suis (1637). cōgitāre 'to think' survives in Spanish cuidar 'to look after' and Romanian cugeta 'to ponder'.
Motto of the Benedictine monks, summing up the Rule of St Benedict (6th c.), though the phrase itself is later. labōrāre 'to toil' → Italian lavorare, French labourer 'to plough'.
From Vergil, Georgics 3.284: sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus, 'but meanwhile it flies, time flies beyond recall'. tempus → Italian tempo, Spanish tiempo, French temps, Romanian timp.

A medieval monastic motto. Tertullian (Apologeticum 33) tells of the voice that reminded a general in his triumph: respice post tē! hominem tē mementō! 'look behind you! remember you are a man!'. mementō is the imperative of meminī 'remember'.
A proverb: Pliny the Elder (Natural History 14.141) calls it a common saying, and the Greek poet Alcaeus already said 'wine and truth'. vēritās → Italian verità, Spanish verdad, French vérité.
Terence, Phormio 203 (161 BC). Pliny the Elder said it as he sailed towards erupting Vesuvius (Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16). adiuvāre 'to help' → Italian aiutare, Spanish ayudar, French aider.
After Vegetius, Epitoma reī mīlitāris 3, preface (c. AD 400): quī dēsīderat pācem, praeparet bellum. vīs 'you want' comes from volō, velle; pāx → Italian pace, Spanish paz, French paix.

The Latin form of the first aphorism of Hippocrates (Greek ho bíos brachýs, hē dè téchnē makrḗ), quoted by Seneca, De brevitate vītae 1.1. ars here means the craft of medicine. The verb est is understood.
Vergil, Eclogues 10.69: omnia vincit Amor: et nōs cēdāmus Amōrī, 'love conquers all; let us too yield to love'. omnia is the object, amor the subject: word order is free in Latin.
Seneca, Moral Letters 7.8. docēre 'to teach' → English docile, doctor; discere 'to learn' → English disciple.

Pliny the Elder (Natural History 35.84) says the painter Apelles never let a day pass without drawing at least one line, and this became a proverb. līnea, from līnum 'flax, thread' → Italian linea, Spanish línea, French ligne, English line.

title: Hail Mary
author: Traditional (Latin liturgy)
source: Luke 1:28 and 1:42, with a late-medieval petition; form of the Roman Breviary of 1568
intro: The Hail Mary joins two greetings from the Gospel of Luke, the angel Gabriel's (1:28) and Elizabeth's (1:42), with a petition added in the late Middle Ages; this form was fixed in the Roman Breviary of 1568. It is short and full of words that live on in every Romance language. The translations give the traditional prayer in each language.

tr.en: Hail Mary, full of grace,
tr.it: Ave, o Maria, piena di grazia,
tr.es: Dios te salve, María, llena eres de gracia,
tr.fr: Je vous salue, Marie, pleine de grâce,
tr.pt: Ave Maria, cheia de graça,
tr.ro: Bucură-te, Marie, cea plină de har,

tr.en: the Lord is with thee.
tr.it: il Signore è con te.
tr.es: el Señor es contigo.
tr.fr: le Seigneur est avec vous.
tr.pt: o Senhor é convosco.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. f.

tr.en: Blessed art thou among women,
tr.it: Tu sei benedetta fra le donne
tr.es: Bendita tú eres entre todas las mujeres,
tr.fr: Vous êtes bénie entre toutes les femmes,
tr.pt: Bendita sois vós entre as mulheres,

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. m.

tr.en: and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
tr.it: e benedetto è il frutto del tuo seno, Gesù.
tr.es: y bendito es el fruto de tu vientre, Jesús.
tr.fr: et Jésus, le fruit de vos entrailles, est béni.
tr.pt: e bendito é o fruto do vosso ventre, Jesus.
tr.ro: și binecuvântat este rodul trupului tău, Isus.

tr.en: Holy Mary, Mother of God,
tr.it: Santa Maria, Madre di Dio,
tr.es: Santa María, Madre de Dios,
tr.fr: Sainte Marie, Mère de Dieu,
tr.pt: Santa Maria, Mãe de Deus,

tr.en: pray for us sinners,
tr.it: prega per noi peccatori,
tr.es: ruega por nosotros, pecadores,
tr.fr: priez pour nous, pauvres pécheurs,
tr.pt: rogai por nós, pecadores,

tr.en: now and at the hour of our death.
tr.it: adesso e nell'ora della nostra morte.
tr.es: ahora y en la hora de nuestra muerte.
tr.fr: maintenant et à l'heure de notre mort.
tr.pt: agora e na hora de nossa morte.
tr.ro: acum și în ceasul morții noastre.

tr.en: Amen.
tr.it: Amen.
tr.es: Amén.
tr.fr: Amen.
tr.pt: Amém.

notes.n: Avē is the imperative of aveō 'be well', an everyday Roman greeting ('hail!'). grātiā plēna 'full of grace': plēnus takes the ablative. plēnus → Italian pieno, Spanish lleno, French plein, Portuguese cheio, Romanian plin.

tēcum = tē + cum: with personal pronouns, cum is attached at the end (mēcum, nōbīscum). Spanish contigo and conmigo continue tēcum and mēcum, with an extra con- in front. dominus 'lord, master' → Romanian domn 'lord, sir', Spanish dueño 'owner' and the title don.

benedictus 'blessed' is literally 'well spoken of' (bene + dīcō) → Italian benedetto, Spanish bendito, French béni. Romanian binecuvântat is built the same way from bine 'well' and cuvânt 'word' (from conventus). mulier 'woman' → Spanish mujer, Portuguese mulher, Italian moglie 'wife', Romanian muiere.
frūctus 'fruit' (4th declension) → Italian frutto, Spanish fruto, French fruit. venter 'belly, womb' → Italian ventre, Spanish vientre, French ventre.
Māter Deī: Deī is the genitive of deus, 'of God'. Romanian Dumnezeu 'God' comes from Domine Deus 'Lord God'.
ōrā 'pray' is an imperative (→ Spanish orar). prō + ablative means 'for, on behalf of'. peccātor 'sinner' → Italian peccatore, Spanish pecador, French pécheur; peccātum 'sin' → Romanian păcat.
hōra → Italian ora, Spanish and Portuguese hora, French heure. mors, mortis 'death' → Italian and Portuguese morte, Spanish muerte, French mort, Romanian moarte.

title: The Gods of Olympus
author: Stemma
intro: A first tour of the Roman gods, whom the Romans identified with the Greek gods of Olympus. Their names still live on in planets, in everyday words and in the Romance days of the week. Most of the text uses only the 1st and 2nd declensions.

tr.en: The Romans worship many gods and many goddesses.
tr.it: I Romani venerano molti dèi e molte dee.
tr.es: Los romanos veneran a muchos dioses y muchas diosas.

tr.en: The gods live on Olympus; Olympus is in Greece.
tr.it: Gli dèi abitano sull'Olimpo; l'Olimpo è in Grecia.
tr.es: Los dioses viven en el Olimpo; el Olimpo está en Grecia.

tr.en: Jupiter is king of the gods; he reigns in the sky.
tr.it: Giove è il re degli dèi; regna nel cielo.
tr.es: Júpiter es el rey de los dioses; reina en el cielo.

tr.en: Juno is Jupiter's wife and queen of the gods.
tr.it: Giunone è la moglie di Giove e la regina degli dèi.
tr.es: Juno es la esposa de Júpiter y la reina de los dioses.

tr.en: Neptune lives in the waves and loves horses.
tr.it: Nettuno abita tra le onde e ama i cavalli.
tr.es: Neptuno vive entre las olas y ama a los caballos.

tr.en: Mars is the god of war; Venus is the goddess of love.
tr.it: Marte è il dio della guerra; Venere è la dea dell'amore.
tr.es: Marte es el dios de la guerra; Venus es la diosa del amor.

tr.en: Minerva is the goddess of wisdom and of war.
tr.it: Minerva è la dea della sapienza e della guerra.
tr.es: Minerva es la diosa de la sabiduría y de la guerra.

tr.en: Apollo is the god of poets and doctors.
tr.it: Apollo è il dio dei poeti e dei medici.
tr.es: Apolo es el dios de los poetas y de los médicos.

tr.en: Diana is the goddess of the woods and of the moon; she carries arrows.
tr.it: Diana è la dea dei boschi e della luna; porta le frecce.
tr.es: Diana es la diosa de los bosques y de la luna; lleva flechas.

tr.en: Mercury is the messenger of the gods; he flies swiftly.
tr.it: Mercurio è il messaggero degli dèi; vola veloce.
tr.es: Mercurio es el mensajero de los dioses; vuela veloz.

tr.en: Vulcan is a smith; he makes the weapons of the gods.
tr.it: Vulcano è un fabbro; fabbrica le armi degli dèi.
tr.es: Vulcano es herrero; fabrica las armas de los dioses.

tr.en: Ceres gives grain to the farmers.
tr.it: Cerere dà il grano agli agricoltori.
tr.es: Ceres da el grano a los agricultores.

tr.en: Vesta looks after the hearth and the family.
tr.it: Vesta protegge il focolare e la famiglia.
tr.es: Vesta cuida del hogar y de la familia.

tr.en: Bacchus is the god of wine and of joy.
tr.it: Bacco è il dio del vino e della gioia.
tr.es: Baco es el dios del vino y de la alegría.

tr.en: The Romans build temples for the gods and give them gifts.
tr.it: I Romani costruiscono templi per gli dèi e offrono loro doni.
tr.es: Los romanos construyen templos a los dioses y les ofrecen dones.

notes.n: The Romans identified their gods with the Greek ones: Iuppiter = Zeus, Iūnō = Hera, Neptūnus = Poseidon, Mārs = Ares, Venus = Aphrodite, Minerva = Athena, Diāna = Artemis, Mercurius = Hermes, Vulcānus = Hephaestus, Cerēs = Demeter, Vesta = Hestia, Bacchus = Dionysus; Apollō kept his Greek name. colere 'to tend, worship' gave English cult and culture.
Olympus is a real mountain in northern Greece. in + ablative means 'in' or 'on'.
rēx 'king' → Italian re, Spanish rey, French roi, Portuguese rei; rēgnāre → regnare, reinar, régner.

Iuppiter (Iou-pater, 'Sky-Father', the same name as Greek Zeus patēr) has the irregular genitive Iovis. Iovis diēs 'Jupiter's day' → Italian giovedì, Spanish jueves, French jeudi, Romanian joi 'Thursday'.

Mārtis diēs → martedì, martes, mardi, marți 'Tuesday'; Veneris diēs → venerdì, viernes, vendredi, vineri 'Friday'. bellum was replaced by a Germanic word, *werra: Italian and Spanish guerra, French guerre.
poēta is a masculine noun of the 1st declension, like agricola and nauta. medicus 'doctor' → Italian medico, Spanish médico.
lūna → Italian and Spanish luna, French lune, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună; Lūnae diēs → lunedì, lunes, lundi, luni 'Monday'.
Mercuriī diēs → mercoledì, miércoles, mercredi, miercuri 'Wednesday'. volāre 'to fly' → Italian volare, Spanish volar, French voler.
faber 'craftsman, smith' → Italian fabbro. fabricāre → Italian fabbricare, Spanish fabricar and, worn down by sound change, French forger 'to forge'. Vulcānus gave English volcano.
agricolīs is dative: 'to the farmers'. Cerēs gave English cereal (Cereālis 'of Ceres').
focus 'hearth' became the everyday word for 'fire': Italian fuoco, Spanish fuego, French feu, Portuguese fogo, Romanian foc. Spanish hogar 'home' comes from focāris 'of the hearth'.
deīs is dative plural: 'for the gods'. dōnum 'gift' → Italian dono, Spanish don.

title: Androcles and the Lion
author: Stemma
intro: A runaway slave, a wounded lion and a reunion in the arena. Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights 5.14, 2nd century AD) tells the story on the authority of the Greek writer Apion, who claimed to have watched the scene in Rome; Gellius calls the slave Androclus, the name better known as Androcles. The last line is Gellius's own.

tr.en: Androclus, a Roman slave, lived with his master in Africa.
tr.it: Androclo, uno schiavo romano, viveva con il suo padrone in Africa.
tr.es: Androclo, un esclavo romano, vivía con su amo en África.

tr.en: Because his master beat him every day, Androclus fled into the wilderness.
tr.it: Poiché il padrone lo picchiava ogni giorno, Androclo fuggì nel deserto.
tr.es: Como su amo lo azotaba todos los días, Androclo huyó al desierto.

tr.en: There he went into a cave and hid.
tr.it: Lì entrò in una grotta e si nascose.
tr.es: Allí entró en una cueva y se escondió.

tr.en: Suddenly a great lion with a bleeding paw came into the cave.
tr.it: All'improvviso un grande leone, che aveva una zampa insanguinata, entrò nella grotta.
tr.es: De repente un gran león, que tenía una pata ensangrentada, entró en la cueva.

tr.en: The lion was groaning, and it showed its paw to the slave.
tr.it: Il leone gemeva e mostrò la zampa allo schiavo.
tr.es: El león gemía y le mostró la pata al esclavo.

tr.en: Although he was afraid, Androclus pulled the thorn out of the paw and cleaned the wound.
tr.it: Androclo, benché avesse paura, estrasse la spina dalla zampa e pulì la ferita.
tr.es: Androclo, aunque tenía miedo, sacó la espina de la pata y limpió la herida.

tr.en: After that, the lion and the man lived together in the cave for three years.
tr.it: In seguito il leone e l'uomo vissero insieme nella grotta per tre anni.
tr.es: Después, el león y el hombre vivieron juntos en la cueva durante tres años.

tr.en: Every day the lion gave the slave a share of its prey.
tr.it: Ogni giorno il leone dava allo schiavo una parte della preda.
tr.es: Cada día el león le daba al esclavo una parte de su presa.

tr.en: At last Androclus left the cave, but soldiers caught him and sent him to Rome.
tr.it: Alla fine Androclo lasciò la grotta, ma dei soldati lo catturarono e lo mandarono a Roma.
tr.es: Por fin Androclo dejó la cueva, pero unos soldados lo capturaron y lo enviaron a Roma.

tr.en: There his master had him condemned to the wild beasts.
tr.it: Lì il padrone lo fece condannare alle belve.
tr.es: Allí su amo lo hizo condenar a las fieras.

tr.en: In the Circus Maximus many Romans, and the emperor himself, were watching.
tr.it: Nel Circo Massimo molti Romani, e lo stesso imperatore, stavano a guardare.
tr.es: En el Circo Máximo muchos romanos, y el propio emperador, estaban mirando.

tr.en: Suddenly a huge lion ran into the arena.
tr.it: All'improvviso un leone enorme corse nell'arena.
tr.es: De repente un león enorme salió corriendo a la arena.

tr.en: But when it saw Androclus, it stopped and, like a dog, began licking his hands.
tr.it: Ma quando vide Androclo, si fermò e, come un cane, gli leccava le mani.
tr.es: Pero cuando vio a Androclo, se detuvo y, como un perro, le lamía las manos.

tr.en: Everyone was amazed; the emperor set the slave free and gave him the lion.
tr.it: Tutti erano stupiti; l'imperatore liberò lo schiavo e gli donò il leone.
tr.es: Todos estaban asombrados; el emperador liberó al esclavo y le regaló el león.

tr.en: Afterwards Androclus used to walk through the city with the lion, and people would say:
tr.it: In seguito Androclo passeggiava per la città con il leone, e la gente diceva:
tr.es: Después Androclo paseaba por la ciudad con el león, y la gente decía:

tr.en: “This is the lion who was host to a man; this is the man who was doctor to a lion.”
tr.it: «Questo è il leone che ospitò un uomo, questo è l'uomo che curò un leone.»
tr.es: «Este es el león que dio hospedaje a un hombre, este es el hombre que curó a un león.»

notes.n: dominus 'master, owner' → Spanish dueño 'owner' and the title don, Portuguese dom. Āfrica here is the Roman province, roughly modern Tunisia.
quod 'because' gives the reason. cotīdiē 'every day' (from quot diēs) → Italian quotidiano, Spanish cotidiano 'daily'.
leō, leōnis 'lion' → Italian leone, Spanish león, French lion, Romanian leu (also the name of the currency). pēs, pedis 'foot' → Italian piede, Spanish pie, French pied.
quamquam 'although'. Gellius actually speaks of a huge splinter (stirps); later retellings turned it into a thorn (spīna → Italian spina, Spanish espina, French épine).
trēs annōs is an accusative of duration: 'for three years'. simul 'together': Italian insieme and French ensemble come from in + simul.
praeda 'prey, booty' → Italian preda, Spanish presa, French proie, Romanian pradă.
damnāre ad bēstiās: to condemn someone to face wild beasts in the arena, a common punishment for runaway slaves.
Caesar here simply means 'the emperor'. The title lives on in German Kaiser and Russian tsar.
arēna means 'sand': the floor of the arena was strewn with it. Spanish arena still means 'sand'.
ubi + perfect: 'when it saw'. manus 'hand' (4th declension, accusative plural manūs) → Italian and Spanish mano, French main, Romanian mână.
Gellius's own words (Noctes Atticae 5.14.30). hospes means both 'host' and 'guest', and so do Italian ospite and French hôte.

title: Arachne and Minerva
author: Stemma
intro: A weaving contest between a mortal girl and the goddess of crafts, retold after Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.1–145. Arachne's pride costs her dearly, and explains why spiders weave. Arachne's challenge and the goddess's last words are almost exactly Ovid's.

tr.en: In Lydia there lived a girl named Arachne, who wove superbly.
tr.it: In Lidia viveva una fanciulla di nome Aracne, che tesseva benissimo.
tr.es: En Lidia vivía una muchacha llamada Aracne, que tejía de maravilla.

tr.en: Nymphs used to come to her and admire her work.
tr.it: Le ninfe venivano da lei e ammiravano i suoi lavori.
tr.es: Las ninfas venían a verla y admiraban sus obras.

tr.en: “Minerva taught you!” they would say.
tr.it: «Ti ha insegnato Minerva!» dicevano.
tr.es: «¡Te ha enseñado Minerva!», decían.

tr.en: But proud Arachne replied: “Nobody taught me; I am better than Minerva!”
tr.it: Ma la superba Aracne rispose: «Nessuno mi ha insegnato; io sono più brava di Minerva!»
tr.es: Pero la orgullosa Aracne respondió: «Nadie me ha enseñado; ¡soy mejor que Minerva!»

tr.en: Minerva, who had heard everything, came to the girl in the guise of an old woman.
tr.it: Minerva, che aveva sentito tutto, si presentò alla fanciulla sotto l'aspetto di una vecchia.
tr.es: Minerva, que lo había oído todo, se presentó ante la muchacha con el aspecto de una anciana.

tr.en: “Give way to the goddess, girl,” she said, “and ask for her pardon!”
tr.it: «Cedi alla dea, ragazza», disse, «e chiedi perdono!»
tr.es: «Cede ante la diosa, muchacha», dijo, «¡y pide perdón!»

tr.en: Arachne replied angrily: “Why doesn't she come herself? Why does she avoid a contest?”
tr.it: Aracne rispose adirata: «Perché non viene lei stessa? Perché evita la gara?»
tr.es: Aracne respondió enfadada: «¿Por qué no viene ella misma? ¿Por qué evita el certamen?»

tr.en: Then Minerva said, “Here she comes!” and showed her true form.
tr.it: Allora Minerva disse: «Eccola che viene!», e mostrò il suo vero aspetto.
tr.es: Entonces Minerva dijo: «¡Aquí viene!», y mostró su verdadera forma.

tr.en: Then both sat down and wove for a long time.
tr.it: Poi entrambe si sedettero e tesserono a lungo.
tr.es: Después ambas se sentaron y tejieron largo tiempo.

tr.en: Minerva wove the gods in their glory, Arachne the misdeeds of the gods.
tr.it: Minerva tessé gli dèi nella loro gloria, Aracne le colpe degli dèi.
tr.es: Minerva tejió a los dioses en su gloria; Aracne, las culpas de los dioses.

tr.en: The girl's work was most beautiful; the goddess could find no flaw in it.
tr.it: Il lavoro della fanciulla era bellissimo; la dea non riusciva a trovarvi alcun difetto.
tr.es: La obra de la muchacha era bellísima; la diosa no podía encontrarle ningún defecto.

tr.en: In her anger Minerva tore the tapestry and struck the girl with her shuttle.
tr.it: Minerva, furiosa, strappò la tela e colpì la fanciulla con la spola.
tr.es: Minerva, furiosa, rasgó la tela y golpeó a la muchacha con la lanzadera.

tr.en: Poor Arachne hanged herself with a noose.
tr.it: La povera Aracne si impiccò con un cappio.
tr.es: La pobre Aracne se ahorcó con un lazo.

tr.en: Then the goddess turned her into a spider: “Live, yes, but hang, you wicked girl!”
tr.it: Allora la dea la trasformò in un ragno: «Vivi pure, ma resta appesa, sfrontata!»
tr.es: Entonces la diosa la convirtió en araña: «¡Vive, sí, pero cuelga, insolente!»

tr.en: Even now the spider hangs and weaves.
tr.it: Ancora oggi il ragno sta appeso e tesse.
tr.es: Todavía hoy la araña cuelga y teje.

notes.n: nōmine 'by name' is an ablative of nōmen. texere 'to weave' → Italian tessere, Spanish tejer, English textile and text: a text is something 'woven' out of words. optimē is the superlative of bene.
opera is the plural of opus 'work', the source of Italian (and English) opera. mīrārī 'to admire' is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning; Spanish mirar 'to look' comes from it.
melior 'better' is the comparative of bonus; quam means 'than'. Romance kept it: Italian migliore, Spanish mejor, French meilleur, Portuguese melhor. nēmō 'nobody' = ne + homō.
anus, anūs (4th declension) means 'old woman'. speciē anūs 'in the appearance of an old woman' is an ablative of manner.
cēdere 'to give way to' takes the dative: cēde deae. venia 'pardon' → Italian venia, English venial.
Almost Ovid's own words (Met. 6.42): cūr nōn venit ipsa? cūr haec certāmina vītat? venit with a short e is present ('comes'); vēnit is perfect ('came').
In Ovid (Met. 6.43) the goddess answers with the same word: 'venit' ait, 'she is here,' and throws off her disguise.
Arachne wove the gods' misdeeds: Jupiter as a bull carrying off Europa, as a swan with Leda, and many more. crīmen 'charge, crime' → English crime.

tēla 'web, cloth on the loom' → Italian and Spanish tela 'cloth', French toile (whence toilette and English toilet). radius was the weaver's shuttle, but also a rod, a wheel's spoke and a ray: English radius and radio.
Ovid's line (Met. 6.136): vīve quidem, pende tamen, improba. arānea 'spider' → Italian ragno, Spanish araña, French araignée, Portuguese aranha; Greek arachnē 'spider' gives English arachnid.

title: Daedalus and Icarus
author: Stemma
intro: The story of the first flight and the first fall, retold after Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183–235. Daedalus, the master craftsman who built the Labyrinth for King Minos, escapes from Crete on wings of feathers and wax. The imperfect paints the scene, the perfect moves the story on, and a few phrases are Ovid's own.

tr.en: Daedalus, a famous craftsman, lived on Crete with his son Icarus.
tr.it: Dedalo, un celebre artefice, viveva a Creta con il figlio Icaro.
tr.es: Dédalo, un célebre artesano, vivía en Creta con su hijo Ícaro.

tr.en: King Minos kept them on the island, and Daedalus longed for his homeland.
tr.it: Il re Minosse li tratteneva sull'isola, e Dedalo aveva nostalgia della patria.
tr.es: El rey Minos los retenía en la isla, y Dédalo añoraba su patria.

tr.en: “Minos holds the lands and the waves,” he said, “but he does not hold the sky.”
tr.it: «Minosse possiede le terre e le onde», disse, «ma non possiede il cielo.»
tr.es: «Minos domina las tierras y las olas», dijo, «pero no domina el cielo.»

tr.en: So he joined feathers together with thread and wax and made wings.
tr.it: Così unì delle penne con filo e cera e fece delle ali.
tr.es: Así que unió plumas con hilo y cera e hizo unas alas.

tr.en: The boy Icarus was laughing and playing with the feathers.
tr.it: Il piccolo Icaro rideva e giocava con le penne.
tr.es: El niño Ícaro reía y jugaba con las plumas.

tr.en: Then Daedalus warned his son: “Fly between the waves and the sun, Icarus!”
tr.it: Poi Dedalo avvertì il figlio: «Vola tra le onde e il sole, Icaro!»
tr.es: Luego Dédalo advirtió a su hijo: «¡Vuela entre las olas y el sol, Ícaro!»

tr.en: “For the waves weigh the feathers down, and the sun melts the wax.”
tr.it: «Perché le onde appesantiscono le penne, e il sole scioglie la cera.»
tr.es: «Porque las olas hacen pesadas las plumas, y el sol derrite la cera.»

tr.en: Father and son moved their wings and flew up into the sky.
tr.it: Padre e figlio mossero le ali e volarono in cielo.
tr.es: Padre e hijo movieron las alas y volaron hacia el cielo.

tr.en: A fisherman and a shepherd saw them and were amazed: “They are gods!”
tr.it: Un pescatore e un pastore li videro e rimasero stupiti: «Sono dèi!»
tr.es: Un pescador y un pastor los vieron y se quedaron atónitos: «¡Son dioses!»

tr.en: But Icarus, because he loved flying, left his father and flew higher.
tr.it: Ma Icaro, poiché godeva a volare, lasciò il padre e volò più in alto.
tr.es: Pero Ícaro, porque disfrutaba volando, dejó a su padre y voló más alto.

tr.en: The sun softened the wax, and the feathers fell from the wings.
tr.it: Il sole ammorbidì la cera, e le penne caddero dalle ali.
tr.es: El sol ablandó la cera, y las plumas cayeron de las alas.

tr.en: Icarus called out to his father, but he fell into the blue sea.
tr.it: Icaro chiamò il padre, ma cadde nel mare azzurro.
tr.es: Ícaro llamó a su padre, pero cayó al mar azul.

tr.en: But the unhappy father, a father no longer, kept crying: “Icarus, where are you?”
tr.it: Ma il padre infelice, ormai non più padre, gridava: «Icaro, dove sei?»
tr.es: Pero el padre desdichado, que ya no era padre, gritaba: «Ícaro, ¿dónde estás?»

tr.en: At last he saw the feathers on the waves, and he buried his son's body on an island.
tr.it: Alla fine vide le penne sulle onde e seppellì il corpo del figlio su un'isola.
tr.es: Por fin vio las plumas sobre las olas y enterró el cuerpo de su hijo en una isla.

tr.en: That island is still called Icaria today.
tr.it: Quell'isola ancora oggi si chiama Icaria.
tr.es: Esa isla todavía hoy se llama Icaria.

notes.n: artifex 'craftsman, artist' (ars + faciō 'make') → Italian artefice, English artifice.
patria 'fatherland', from pater → Italian and Spanish patria, French patrie. dēsīderāre 'to long for, miss' → Italian desiderare, French désirer, English desire.
Ovid's version (Met. 8.187): omnia possideat, nōn possidet āera Mīnōs, 'Minos may own everything, but he does not own the air'.
penna 'feather' → Italian penna 'feather, pen', English pen (a quill). cēra 'wax' → Italian and Spanish cera, French cire, Romanian ceară. āla 'wing' → Italian and Spanish ala, French aile.
The imperfects rīdēbat and lūdēbat paint the background: what the boy kept doing while his father worked.
volā is the imperative of volō, volāre 'to fly', not of volō, velle 'to want'. monuit is the perfect of moneō 'warn' (cf. English admonish).
mōvērunt is the perfect of moveō; the perfect stem has a long vowel (mōvī).
quod 'because' gives a reason. altius 'higher' is the comparative of the adverb altē 'high'.
cecidērunt is the perfect of cadō 'fall', with a doubled first syllable (ce-cid-ī). cadere → Italian cadere, Spanish caer, Portuguese cair, Romanian cădea.
mare 'sea' → Italian mare, Spanish and Portuguese mar, French mer, Romanian mare.
Ovid's own words (Met. 8.231–2): at pater īnfēlīx, nec iam pater, 'Īcare,' dīxit, 'Īcare,' dīxit, 'ubi es?'
The island of Icaria in the eastern Aegean, and the Icarian Sea, were said to be named after the boy. appellātur is passive: 'is called'.

title: Gaudeamus
author: Anonymous (student song)
source: De brevitāte vītae, stanzas 1–2, in the version printed by C. W. Kindleben (1781)
intro: The best-known student song in Europe, still sung at university ceremonies. Its words and tune took their present shape in 18th-century Germany (the text was printed by C. W. Kindleben in 1781), but it grew out of medieval Latin verses on the shortness of life. These are the first two stanzas; the song exists in many slightly different versions.

tr.en: So let us rejoice,
tr.it: Rallegriamoci dunque,
tr.es: Alegrémonos, pues,

tr.en: while we are young.
tr.it: finché siamo giovani.
tr.es: mientras somos jóvenes.

tr.en: After pleasant youth,
tr.it: Dopo la gioiosa giovinezza,
tr.es: Tras la alegre juventud,

tr.en: after troublesome old age,
tr.it: dopo la molesta vecchiaia,
tr.es: tras la penosa vejez,

tr.en: the earth will have us.
tr.it: ci avrà la terra.
tr.es: nos tendrá la tierra.

tr.en: Where are those who before us
tr.it: Dove sono coloro che prima di noi
tr.es: ¿Dónde están los que antes que nosotros

tr.en: were in the world?
tr.it: furono al mondo?
tr.es: estuvieron en el mundo?

tr.en: Go up to the heavens,
tr.it: Salite al cielo,
tr.es: Subid al cielo,

tr.en: cross over to the underworld,
tr.it: scendete agli inferi,
tr.es: bajad a los infiernos,

tr.en: where they have already gone.
tr.it: dove essi sono già andati.
tr.es: adonde ellos ya se fueron.

notes.n: Gaudeāmus 'let us rejoice' is a present subjunctive of exhortation (1st person plural). gaudium 'joy' → French joie, Italian gioia, Spanish gozo.
iuvenēs dum sumus = dum iuvenēs sumus: the conjunction is moved for the rhythm. iuvenis → Italian giovane, Spanish joven, French jeune.
iuventūs 'youth' and senectūs 'old age' are 3rd-declension feminines in -tūs, -tūtis, like virtūs. iūcundus 'pleasant' → Italian giocondo.
molestus 'troublesome' → Italian molesto, English molest. The everyday Romance words for 'old age' come instead from vetulus 'oldish': Italian vecchiaia, Spanish vejez.
humus 'earth, soil' is feminine although it ends in -us. habēbit is future: 'will have, will hold'. Latin homō 'human being' is related: literally 'earthling'.
Ubi sunt quī ante nōs…? 'Where are those who went before us?' is a favourite theme of medieval poetry, known simply as ubi sunt.
fuēre = fuērunt: -ēre is a shorter, poetic ending of the 3rd person plural perfect.

superī 'those above' (the gods, the heavens) and īnferī 'those below' (the dead) are adjectives used as nouns. vādere 'to go' supplies parts of the Romance verb 'go': Italian vado, Spanish voy, va, French je vais, il va.

ubi iam fuēre 'where they have already been' answers the question ubi sunt…?: those who lived before us are now to be found only among the gods above or the dead below. fuēre is again the short form of fuērunt.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
author: Stemma
intro: In 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army, elephants and all, from Spain over the Alps into Italy. This retelling follows Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 21.28–38, down to the rock split with fire and vinegar. Look out for the pluperfect (-erat), comparatives and superlatives, and one of Hannibal's speeches in Livy's words.

tr.en: Hannibal, the leader of the Carthaginians, had hated the Romans since boyhood.
tr.it: Annibale, condottiero dei Cartaginesi, odiava i Romani fin da bambino.
tr.es: Aníbal, caudillo de los cartagineses, odiaba a los romanos desde niño.

tr.en: With a great army and many elephants he set out from Spain for Italy.
tr.it: Con un grande esercito e molti elefanti partì dalla Spagna verso l'Italia.
tr.es: Con un gran ejército y muchos elefantes partió de Hispania hacia Italia.

tr.en: First he crossed the river Rhône; he carried the elephants over on rafts.
tr.it: Prima attraversò il fiume Rodano; trasportò gli elefanti su zattere.
tr.es: Primero cruzó el río Ródano; transportó a los elefantes en balsas.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. acc. pl. m.

tr.en: Then he reached the Alps, very high mountains covered with snow.
tr.it: Poi giunse alle Alpi, montagne altissime e coperte di neve.
tr.es: Luego llegó a los Alpes, montañas altísimas y cubiertas de nieve.

tr.en: The soldiers, who had come from hot lands, were afraid of the snow and the cold.
tr.it: I soldati, che venivano da terre calde, temevano la neve e il freddo.
tr.es: Los soldados, que habían venido de tierras cálidas, temían la nieve y el frío.

tr.en: The paths were narrow, and the mountain people hurled rocks down from the cliffs.
tr.it: I sentieri erano stretti, e i montanari scagliavano sassi dalle rupi.
tr.es: Los caminos eran estrechos, y los montañeses arrojaban piedras desde los riscos.

tr.en: Many men and horses fell from the paths into the valleys.
tr.it: Molti uomini e cavalli caddero dai sentieri nelle valli.
tr.es: Muchos hombres y caballos cayeron de los caminos a los valles.

tr.en: On the ninth day they reached the top of the Alps.
tr.it: Il nono giorno raggiunsero la cima delle Alpi.
tr.es: Al noveno día llegaron a la cumbre de los Alpes.

tr.en: There Hannibal showed Italy to his soldiers and said:
tr.it: Lì Annibale mostrò l'Italia ai soldati e disse:
tr.es: Allí Aníbal mostró Italia a sus soldados y dijo:

tr.en: “Now you are climbing over the walls not only of Italy, but of the city of Rome itself!”
tr.it: «Ora state scavalcando le mura non solo dell'Italia, ma anche della città di Roma!»
tr.es: «¡Ahora estáis escalando las murallas no solo de Italia, sino también de la ciudad de Roma!»

tr.en: But going down was much harder than climbing up.
tr.it: Ma scendere era molto più difficile che salire.
tr.es: Pero bajar era mucho más difícil que subir.

tr.en: A huge rock was blocking the path.
tr.it: Un enorme masso bloccava il sentiero.
tr.es: Una roca enorme bloqueaba el camino.

tr.en: Then the soldiers broke the rock with fire and vinegar.
tr.it: Allora i soldati spezzarono la roccia con il fuoco e l'aceto.
tr.es: Entonces los soldados rompieron la roca con fuego y vinagre.

tr.en: So on the fifteenth day Hannibal got over the Alps and came down into Italy.
tr.it: Così, il quindicesimo giorno, Annibale superò le Alpi e scese in Italia.
tr.es: Así, al decimoquinto día, Aníbal superó los Alpes y descendió a Italia.

tr.en: He had lost many soldiers, but now the Romans were in great danger.
tr.it: Aveva perso molti soldati, ma ora i Romani erano in grande pericolo.
tr.es: Había perdido muchos soldados, pero ahora los romanos estaban en gran peligro.

notes.n: ōdī 'I hate' has only perfect-system forms with present meaning, so the pluperfect form ōderat simply means 'he hated'. Livy (21.1) tells how Hannibal's father made him swear hatred of Rome at an altar when he was about nine. Poenī 'Phoenicians' is the Roman name for the Carthaginians (cf. Punic).
profectus est is the perfect of the deponent proficīscor 'set out'. exercitus 'army' (4th declension) → Italian esercito, Spanish ejército.
Livy (21.28) describes how the elephants were ferried across the Rhône on huge rafts covered with earth, so they would think they were still on land.
nix, nivis 'snow' → Italian neve, Spanish nieve, French neige, Portuguese neve, Romanian nea. altissimōs is the superlative of altus: 'very high'.
vēnerant is pluperfect, 'had come'. calidus 'hot' → Italian caldo, French chaud; frīgus 'cold' is related to frīgidus → Italian freddo, Spanish frío, French froid.
angustus 'narrow' → Romanian îngust, Italian angusto; English anguish. Spanish montaña and French montagne come from a form related to montānus 'of the mountains'.
summus 'highest': summae Alpēs means 'the top of the Alps'. Livy: nōnō diē in iugum Alpium perventum est.
Livy 21.35: Hannibal told his men that they were climbing over 'the walls not of Italy only, but of the city of Rome'. moenia means 'city walls'.
multō 'by much' (ablative of degree of difference) goes with comparatives: multō difficilius 'much harder'. difficilius is the comparative of difficilis.
Livy (21.37) says they heated the rock with a huge fire and poured vinegar on it to make it crumble. acētum → Italian aceto; Spanish vinagre and French vinaigre are 'sour wine' (vīnum ācre).
quīntō decimō diē 'on the fifteenth day' is an ablative of time when.
āmīserat 'he had lost' is pluperfect. Rome's great defeats followed: the Trebia (218 BC), Lake Trasimene (217) and Cannae (216).

title: Romulus and Remus
author: Stemma
intro: The founding legend of Rome, retold in simple Latin after Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.3–7. The imperfect (-bat) and the perfect (-vit, -it) appear side by side, together with 3rd-declension nouns such as urbs, rēx and frāter. Romulus' last words are Livy's own.

tr.en: Once upon a time Numitor reigned in the city of Alba Longa.
tr.it: Un tempo Numitore regnava nella città di Alba Longa.
tr.es: Antaño Numitor reinaba en la ciudad de Alba Longa.

tr.en: But Amulius, his brother, seized the throne and drove Numitor out.
tr.it: Ma Amulio, suo fratello, si impadronì del regno e cacciò Numitore.
tr.es: Pero Amulio, su hermano, se apoderó del reino y expulsó a Numitor.

tr.en: Amulius made Numitor's daughter, Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin.
tr.it: Amulio fece della figlia di Numitore, Rea Silvia, una vestale.
tr.es: Amulio hizo vestal a la hija de Numitor, Rea Silvia.

tr.en: But the god Mars loved her, and Rhea gave birth to twins, Romulus and Remus.
tr.it: Ma il dio Marte la amò, e Rea partorì due gemelli, Romolo e Remo.
tr.es: Pero el dios Marte la amó, y Rea dio a luz a dos gemelos, Rómulo y Remo.

tr.en: Amulius, furious, ordered his slaves: “Throw the boys into the Tiber!”
tr.it: Amulio, furioso, ordinò ai servi: «Gettate i bambini nel Tevere!»
tr.es: Amulio, furioso, ordenó a sus esclavos: «¡Arrojad a los niños al Tíber!»

tr.en: The slaves put the boys in a basket, but the river left the basket on the bank.
tr.it: I servi misero i bambini in una cesta, ma il fiume lasciò la cesta sulla riva.
tr.es: Los esclavos pusieron a los niños en una canasta, pero el río dejó la canasta en la orilla.

tr.en: A she-wolf, who was coming down to the river, heard the boys.
tr.it: Una lupa, che scendeva al fiume, sentì i bambini.
tr.es: Una loba, que bajaba al río, oyó a los niños.

tr.en: The wolf did not kill the boys but fed them with her own milk.
tr.it: La lupa non uccise i bambini, ma li nutrì con il suo latte.
tr.es: La loba no mató a los niños, sino que los alimentó con su leche.

tr.en: Then the shepherd Faustulus found the twins and carried them home.
tr.it: Poi il pastore Faustolo trovò i gemelli e li portò a casa.
tr.es: Después el pastor Fáustulo encontró a los gemelos y los llevó a su casa.

tr.en: When the twins had grown up, they killed Amulius and gave the kingdom back to Numitor.
tr.it: Quando i gemelli furono cresciuti, uccisero Amulio e restituirono il regno a Numitore.
tr.es: Cuando los gemelos crecieron, mataron a Amulio y devolvieron el reino a Numitor.

tr.en: Then the twins wanted to found a new city near the Tiber.
tr.it: Poi i gemelli volevano fondare una nuova città vicino al Tevere.
tr.es: Entonces los gemelos querían fundar una nueva ciudad cerca del Tíber.

tr.en: They consulted the gods: Remus saw six vultures, Romulus twelve.
tr.it: Consultarono gli dèi: Remo vide sei avvoltoi, Romolo dodici.
tr.es: Consultaron a los dioses: Remo vio seis buitres, Rómulo doce.

tr.en: Romulus was building walls; Remus, who was mocking his brother, jumped over the new walls.
tr.it: Romolo costruiva le mura; Remo, che derideva il fratello, saltò oltre le nuove mura.
tr.es: Rómulo construía las murallas; Remo, que se burlaba de su hermano, saltó por encima de las nuevas murallas.

tr.en: Then Romulus in his anger killed Remus and said: “So from now on to anyone else who leaps over my walls!”
tr.it: Allora Romolo, adirato, uccise Remo e disse: «Così d'ora in poi a chiunque altro scavalchi le mie mura!»
tr.es: Entonces Rómulo, enfurecido, mató a Remo y dijo: «¡Así, en adelante, a cualquier otro que salte mis murallas!»

tr.en: So Romulus reigned alone and called the city Rome, after his own name.
tr.it: Così Romolo regnò da solo e chiamò la città Roma, dal suo nome.
tr.es: Así Rómulo reinó solo y llamó a la ciudad Roma, por su propio nombre.

notes.n: rēgnābat is imperfect (-bā-): an ongoing state in the past, 'was reigning'. Contrast the perfects occupāvit and expulit in the next line: single, completed events. Alba Longa means 'the long white (town)'.
The Vestals, priestesses of Vesta, were sworn to virginity for thirty years, so Rhea could have no sons to claim the throne.
geminī 'twins' gave English Gemini; Italian gemelli, Spanish gemelos and French jumeaux come from the diminutive gemellus. peperit is the perfect of pariō 'give birth'.
iacite is a plural imperative ('throw!', said to several slaves). Tiberim: a few 3rd-declension nouns (Tiberis, turris, puppis) have the accusative in -im.
rīpa 'bank' → Italian riva, French rive; French rivière and English river come from rīpāria 'of the bank'.

quae … veniēbat is a relative clause: quae agrees with lupa. Livy also gives a down-to-earth version: lupa was slang for a prostitute (cf. Italian lupanare 'brothel'), and the 'wolf' was really the shepherd's wife Larentia.
lac, lactis 'milk' → Italian latte, Spanish leche, French lait, Portuguese leite, Romanian lapte.
pāstor 'shepherd' → Italian pastore, Spanish pastor, French pasteur 'pastor', Romanian păstor.
ubi + perfect means 'when': ubi geminī crēvērunt 'when the twins had grown up'. crēvērunt is the perfect of crēscō 'grow'.
Augury: the Romans read the will of the gods in the flight of birds (auspicium, from avis 'bird' + specere 'watch'). Remus saw his six vultures first, Romulus saw twelve, so each claimed the victory.
These are Livy's own words (1.7.2); a verb such as pereat 'may he perish' is understood. trānsiliet is future: 'will leap over'.
ā nōmine suō 'after his own name'. Tradition dated the founding to 21 April 753 BC, still celebrated as Rome's birthday (Natale di Roma).

title: The Lord's Prayer
author: Gospel of Matthew, in the Latin of the Vulgate and the Roman liturgy
source: Matthew 6:9–13 (Vulgate of St Jerome), liturgical form
intro: The Lord's Prayer as it is said in the Latin liturgy, from Matthew 6:9–13 in St Jerome's Vulgate. Its wishes are present subjunctives (sānctificētur, adveniat, fīat), a form Romanian still uses in exactly the same way. The translations give the traditional prayer in each language.

tr.en: Our Father, who art in heaven,
tr.it: Padre nostro, che sei nei cieli,
tr.es: Padre nuestro, que estás en el cielo,
tr.fr: Notre Père, qui es aux cieux,
tr.pt: Pai nosso, que estais nos céus,
tr.ro: Tatăl nostru, Care ești în ceruri,

tr.en: hallowed be thy name;
tr.it: sia santificato il tuo nome,
tr.es: santificado sea tu nombre;
tr.fr: que ton nom soit sanctifié,
tr.pt: santificado seja o vosso nome;

tr.en: thy kingdom come;
tr.it: venga il tuo regno,
tr.es: venga a nosotros tu reino;
tr.fr: que ton règne vienne,
tr.pt: venha a nós o vosso reino;

tr.en: thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
tr.it: sia fatta la tua volontà, come in cielo così in terra.
tr.es: hágase tu voluntad en la tierra como en el cielo.
tr.fr: que ta volonté soit faite sur la terre comme au ciel.
tr.pt: seja feita a vossa vontade, assim na terra como no céu.
tr.ro: facă-se voia Ta, precum în cer așa și pe pământ.

tr.en: Give us this day our daily bread,
tr.it: Dacci oggi il nostro pane quotidiano,
tr.es: Danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día;
tr.fr: Donne-nous aujourd'hui notre pain de ce jour.
tr.pt: O pão nosso de cada dia nos dai hoje;
tr.ro: Pâinea noastră cea de toate zilele dă-ne-o nouă astăzi;

tr.en: and forgive us our trespasses,
tr.it: e rimetti a noi i nostri debiti
tr.es: perdona nuestras ofensas,
tr.fr: Pardonne-nous nos offenses,
tr.pt: perdoai-nos as nossas ofensas,
tr.ro: și ne iartă nouă greșelile noastre,

tr.en: as we forgive those who trespass against us.
tr.it: come noi li rimettiamo ai nostri debitori,
tr.es: como también nosotros perdonamos a los que nos ofenden;
tr.fr: comme nous pardonnons aussi à ceux qui nous ont offensés.
tr.pt: assim como nós perdoamos a quem nos tem ofendido;
tr.ro: precum și noi iertăm greșiților noștri;

tr.en: And lead us not into temptation,
tr.it: e non ci indurre in tentazione,
tr.es: no nos dejes caer en la tentación,
tr.fr: Et ne nous laisse pas entrer en tentation,
tr.pt: e não nos deixeis cair em tentação,
tr.ro: și nu ne duce pe noi în ispită,

tr.en: but deliver us from evil.
tr.it: ma liberaci dal male.
tr.es: y líbranos del mal.
tr.fr: mais délivre-nous du Mal.
tr.pt: mas livrai-nos do mal.
tr.ro: ci ne izbăvește de cel rău.

tr.en: Amen.
tr.it: Amen.
tr.es: Amén.
tr.fr: Amen.
tr.pt: Amém.

notes.n: Latin normally puts the possessive after the noun, as Italian Padre nostro, Portuguese Pai nosso and Romanian Tatăl nostru still do. Romanian replaced pater with tată, a child's word. caelum is neuter in the singular but masculine in the plural: in caelīs.
sānctificētur, adveniat and fīat are present subjunctives expressing a wish: 'may it be hallowed', 'may it come', 'may it be done'. Romanian keeps exactly this pattern: sfințească-se, vie, facă-se.
rēgnum → Italian regno, Spanish reino, French règne. Romanian împărăție comes from împărat 'emperor', from imperātor.
terra → Italian terra, Spanish tierra, French terre; Romanian pământ comes instead from pavīmentum 'floor, pavement'. Romanian cer continues caelum.

quotīdiānum is the church spelling of classical cotīdiānus 'daily' (from cotīdiē 'every day') → Italian quotidiano, Spanish and Portuguese cotidiano, French quotidien. pānis → Italian pane, Spanish pan, French pain, Portuguese pão, Romanian pâine. dā is the imperative of dō 'give'.
dēbita 'debts': sins are pictured as debts, as in Matthew 6:12; Italian keeps debiti. dīmittere means 'to let go'. Romanian a ierta 'to forgive' comes from Latin lībertāre 'to set free'.
nē + present subjunctive (nē indūcās) is a negative request: 'do not lead'. tentātiō is the church spelling of temptātiō. Romanian ispită is a Slavic loanword.
līberā is an imperative, 'set free!' → Italian liberare, Spanish librar, Portuguese livrar, French délivrer.
Āmēn is a Hebrew word, 'truly, so be it', which came into Latin through Greek.

title: The Trojan Horse
author: Stemma
intro: How Troy fell, retold after Book 2 of Vergil's Aeneid, where Aeneas tells the story to Queen Dido. After ten years of siege the Greeks trick the Trojans with a wooden horse. Notice how the imperfect describes situations while the perfect moves the story on; one line is Vergil's most famous warning.

tr.en: For ten years the Greeks were besieging Troy, but they could not take the city.
tr.it: Per dieci anni i Greci assediarono Troia, ma non riuscivano a prendere la città.
tr.es: Durante diez años los griegos asediaron Troya, pero no podían tomar la ciudad.

tr.en: At last Ulysses, a cunning man, came up with a plan.
tr.it: Alla fine Ulisse, uomo astuto, escogitò un piano.
tr.es: Por fin Ulises, un hombre astuto, ideó un plan.

tr.en: The Greeks built a huge wooden horse and hid soldiers inside it.
tr.it: I Greci costruirono un enorme cavallo di legno e vi nascosero dentro dei soldati.
tr.es: Los griegos construyeron un enorme caballo de madera y escondieron soldados en su interior.

tr.en: The rest of the Greeks sailed to the island of Tenedos and lay hidden there.
tr.it: Gli altri Greci navigarono fino all'isola di Tenedo e lì restavano nascosti.
tr.es: Los demás griegos navegaron hasta la isla de Ténedos y allí permanecían ocultos.

tr.en: The Trojans saw the empty shore and went joyfully out of the gates.
tr.it: I Troiani videro la spiaggia deserta e uscirono felici dalle porte.
tr.es: Los troyanos vieron la playa vacía y salieron contentos por las puertas.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. n.

tr.en: “The Greeks have fled!” they shouted. “The war is over!”
tr.it: «I Greci sono fuggiti!» gridavano. «La guerra è finita!»
tr.es: «¡Los griegos han huido!», gritaban. «¡La guerra ha terminado!»

tr.en: Many gazed at the horse and wanted to bring it into the city.
tr.it: Molti guardavano il cavallo e volevano portarlo in città.
tr.es: Muchos contemplaban el caballo y querían llevarlo a la ciudad.

w: pres. act. ptcp. acc. pl. m.

tr.en: But Laocoön, a priest of Neptune, cried out: “I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts!”
tr.it: Ma Laocoonte, sacerdote di Nettuno, gridò: «Temo i Greci anche quando portano doni!»
tr.es: Pero Laocoonte, sacerdote de Neptuno, gritó: «¡Temo a los griegos incluso cuando traen regalos!»

tr.en: Suddenly two huge serpents came out of the sea and killed Laocoön together with his sons.
tr.it: All'improvviso due enormi serpenti uscirono dal mare e uccisero Laocoonte insieme ai figli.
tr.es: De repente dos enormes serpientes salieron del mar y mataron a Laocoonte junto con sus hijos.

tr.en: The Trojans were frightened and dragged the horse into the city.
tr.it: I Troiani ebbero paura e trascinarono il cavallo in città.
tr.es: Los troyanos tuvieron miedo y arrastraron el caballo a la ciudad.

tr.en: At night the Trojans, happy and tired, were asleep.
tr.it: Di notte i Troiani, felici e stanchi, dormivano.
tr.es: Por la noche los troyanos, felices y cansados, dormían.

tr.en: Then the Greeks secretly climbed down from the horse and opened the gates.
tr.it: Allora i Greci scesero di nascosto dal cavallo e aprirono le porte.
tr.es: Entonces los griegos bajaron a escondidas del caballo y abrieron las puertas.

tr.en: The other Greeks, who had secretly come back, rushed into the city.
tr.it: Gli altri Greci, che erano tornati di nascosto, si precipitarono in città.
tr.es: Los demás griegos, que habían vuelto en secreto, irrumpieron en la ciudad.

tr.en: So the Greeks captured Troy and set it on fire.
tr.it: Così i Greci presero Troia e la incendiarono.
tr.es: Así los griegos tomaron Troya y la incendiaron.

w: pres. act. ptcp. abl. sg. f.

tr.en: Aeneas, however, fled from the burning city with his father and his son.
tr.it: Enea però fuggì dalla città in fiamme con il padre e il figlio.
tr.es: Eneas, sin embargo, huyó de la ciudad en llamas con su padre y su hijo.

notes.n: decem annōs is an accusative of duration: 'for ten years'. poterant is the imperfect of possum 'I can'.
Ulixēs is the Latin name of Odysseus (hence English Ulysses). cōnsilium capere means 'to form a plan'.
ligneus 'wooden', from lignum 'wood' → Italian legno, Spanish leño 'log' and leña 'firewood'. mīles, mīlitis 'soldier' gives English military.
Tenedos is a small island off the coast near Troy; Vergil (Aen. 2.21) says it lay in sight of the city.
ē portīs 'out of the gates': ē is the form of ex used before consonants. porta 'gate' → Italian and Portuguese porta, Spanish puerta, French porte, Romanian poartă.
fūgērunt (long ū) is perfect, 'they have fled'; the present would be fugiunt. fīnītum est: the perfect passive is built from the participle + sum.
Vergil, Aeneid 2.49: timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentēs. et here means 'even'; Danaī is the poets' name for the Greeks. ferentēs is a present participle, 'bringing'.
serpēns is literally 'the creeping one' (serpere 'to creep') → Italian serpente, Romanian șarpe.
nox, noctis 'night' → Italian notte, Spanish noche, French nuit, Portuguese noite, Romanian noapte. Nocte, an ablative of time, means 'at night'.
redierant is pluperfect, 'had come back': the Greek fleet had sailed back from Tenedos in the dark.
ārdente 'burning' is a present participle agreeing with urbe. Aeneas will wander to Italy and become the ancestor of the Romans: the story of the Aeneid.

title: All Gaul
author: Julius Caesar
intro: The opening chapter of Caesar's own account of his conquest of Gaul (58–50 BC), written in the third person in deliberately plain, clear Latin. Before the war begins, he sketches the land and its peoples like a map. Its first sentence is probably the best-known line of Latin prose, and its vocabulary—pars, lingua, lēx, flūmen, mōns, sōl—lives on almost unchanged in the Romance languages.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. f.

tr.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts,
tr.it: La Gallia nel suo insieme è divisa in tre parti,
tr.es: La Galia en su conjunto está dividida en tres partes,

tr.en: of which the Belgae inhabit one, the Aquitani another,
tr.it: delle quali una è abitata dai Belgi, un'altra dagli Aquitani,
tr.es: de las cuales una la habitan los belgas, otra los aquitanos,

tr.en: and the third those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls.
tr.it: la terza coloro che nella loro lingua si chiamano Celti, nella nostra Galli.
tr.es: y la tercera los que en su propia lengua se llaman celtas y en la nuestra galos.

tr.en: All these differ from one another in language, customs and laws.
tr.it: Tutti costoro differiscono tra loro per lingua, istituzioni e leggi.
tr.es: Todos ellos se diferencian entre sí por la lengua, las instituciones y las leyes.

tr.en: The river Garonne separates the Gauls from the Aquitani; the Marne and the Seine separate them from the Belgae.
tr.it: Il fiume Garonna separa i Galli dagli Aquitani, la Marna e la Senna dai Belgi.
tr.es: El río Garona separa a los galos de los aquitanos; el Marne y el Sena, de los belgas.

tr.en: Of all these the bravest are the Belgae,
tr.it: Di tutti questi i più valorosi sono i Belgi,
tr.es: De todos ellos, los más valientes son los belgas,

tr.en: because they are farthest from the civilization and refinement of the Province,
tr.it: perché sono i più lontani dalla civiltà e dalla raffinatezza della Provincia,
tr.es: porque son los que están más lejos de la civilización y el refinamiento de la Provincia,

tr.en: and merchants very seldom visit them and bring in the things that tend to make men's spirits soft,
tr.it: e assai di rado i mercanti si recano da loro a importare ciò che serve a infiacchire gli animi,
tr.es: y rarísima vez llegan hasta ellos los mercaderes para introducir lo que sirve para afeminar los ánimos,

tr.en: and they are nearest to the Germans, who live across the Rhine, with whom they are continually at war.
tr.it: e sono vicinissimi ai Germani, che abitano al di là del Reno, con i quali combattono senza sosta.
tr.es: y son los más próximos a los germanos, que habitan al otro lado del Rin, con quienes están continuamente en guerra.

tr.en: For this reason the Helvetii too surpass the rest of the Gauls in courage,
tr.it: Per questo motivo anche gli Elvezi superano in valore gli altri Galli,
tr.es: Por esta razón también los helvecios superan en valor a los demás galos,

tr.en: because they fight the Germans in almost daily battles,
tr.it: perché combattono contro i Germani in scontri quasi quotidiani,
tr.es: porque luchan con los germanos en combates casi diarios,

tr.en: when they either keep them out of their own territory or themselves wage war in theirs.
tr.it: quando o li tengono lontani dal proprio territorio o fanno essi stessi la guerra nel loro.
tr.es: cuando o bien los rechazan de su propio territorio o bien hacen ellos mismos la guerra en el de aquellos.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. n.

tr.en: Of these lands, the one part which, as has been said, the Gauls occupy begins at the river Rhône;
tr.it: Di queste terre, la parte che, come si è detto, occupano i Galli comincia dal fiume Rodano;
tr.es: De estas tierras, la parte que, como se ha dicho, ocupan los galos empieza en el río Ródano;

tr.en: it is bounded by the river Garonne, the Ocean and the territory of the Belgae;
tr.it: è delimitata dal fiume Garonna, dall'Oceano e dal territorio dei Belgi;
tr.es: está limitada por el río Garona, el Océano y el territorio de los belgas;

tr.en: on the side of the Sequani and the Helvetii it also reaches the river Rhine; it faces north.
tr.it: dalla parte dei Sequani e degli Elvezi tocca anche il fiume Reno; è rivolta a settentrione.
tr.es: por el lado de los secuanos y los helvecios llega también al río Rin; está orientada al norte.

tr.en: The Belgae begin at the farthest borders of Gaul and reach to the lower part of the river Rhine;
tr.it: I Belgi cominciano dagli estremi confini della Gallia e arrivano fino al corso inferiore del Reno;
tr.es: Los belgas comienzan en los confines extremos de la Galia y llegan hasta el curso inferior del Rin;

tr.en: they face the north and the rising sun.
tr.it: guardano a settentrione e al sole nascente.
tr.es: miran hacia el norte y hacia el sol naciente.

tr.en: Aquitania stretches from the river Garonne to the Pyrenees and to that part of the Ocean which lies towards Spain;
tr.it: L'Aquitania si estende dal fiume Garonna ai Pirenei e a quella parte dell'Oceano che si trova verso la Spagna;
tr.es: Aquitania se extiende desde el río Garona hasta los Pirineos y hasta la parte del Océano que da a Hispania;

tr.en: it faces between the setting of the sun and the north.
tr.it: guarda tra il tramonto e settentrione.
tr.es: mira entre el ocaso y el norte.

notes.n: omnis with a singular noun here means 'as a whole, taken all together', not 'every'. dīvīsa est is a perfect passive (participle + est) describing a state: 'is divided'. partēs trēs → Italian tre parti, Spanish tres partes, French trois parties.
quārum 'of which' refers back to partēs. With ūnam … aliam … tertiam supply partem each time; the one verb incolunt serves all three clauses.
quī … appellantur has no expressed antecedent: '(those) who are called'. ipsōrum linguā 'in their own language' is answered by nostrā (linguā) 'in ours'.
inter sē 'among themselves, from one another' is the regular Latin way of saying 'each other'. lēx, lēgis → Italian legge, Spanish ley, French loi; lingua → lingua, lengua, langue.

dīvidit is singular although Mātrona et Sēquana is a double subject: together the two rivers form one boundary. flūmen stands in apposition to Garumna. The modern names Garonne, Marne and Seine continue these Gaulish river names.

longissimē is the superlative of the adverb longē 'far'; absunt is from ab-sum 'be away'. hūmānitās is the polish of civilized life. The Province (prōvincia) is Rome's province in southern Gaul—still called Provence.
minimē … saepe 'least often', i.e. 'very seldom' (minimē is the superlative of parum). ad effēminandōs animōs is ad + gerundive expressing purpose: 'for softening the spirits'.

quibuscum = cum quibus: with personal and relative pronouns cum is attached after the word (mēcum, tēcum, nōbīscum). Spanish conmigo, contigo and Portuguese comigo, contigo continue mēcum, tēcum with con- added again in front.
cum + indicative here means 'when(ever)': it describes what regularly happens, not a cause.

quam Gallōs obtinēre dictum est: an accusative and infinitive depending on the impersonal dictum est 'it has been said': 'which (it has been said) the Gauls hold'. Caesar has said so in his opening sentence.
septentriōnēs are literally the 'seven plough-oxen' (septem triōnēs), the stars of the Great Bear, which mark the north; Italian settentrione and Spanish septentrional still mean 'north(ern)'.
oriuntur 'they arise, begin' is a deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. Its participle, as in orientem sōlem 'the rising sun' in the next line, gives the Orient, Italian and Spanish oriente.

occāsus sōlis 'the setting of the sun' = the west (from occidō 'fall, set', whence also the Occident); Spanish ocaso still means 'sunset'. sōl → Italian sole, Spanish and Portuguese sol; French soleil is from a diminutive *sōliculus.

title: Claim Yourself for Yourself
author: Seneca the Younger
intro: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65), Stoic philosopher and once Nero's tutor, wrote 124 letters to his friend Lucilius in the last years of his life. The very first is about time: the only thing that truly belongs to us, and the one we waste most carelessly. Its short, pointed sentences made Seneca a favourite moralist of the Renaissance, from Petrarch to Montaigne.

tr.en: Do so, my dear Lucilius: claim yourself for yourself,
tr.it: Fa' così, mio Lucilio: rivendica te stesso a te stesso,
tr.es: Hazlo así, querido Lucilio: reclámate para ti mismo,

tr.en: and the time which until now was either taken from you, or stolen, or simply slipped away—gather it and keep it.
tr.it: e il tempo che finora ti veniva tolto, o sottratto, o ti sfuggiva, raccoglilo e custodiscilo.
tr.es: y el tiempo que hasta ahora te arrebataban, te sustraían o se te escapaba, recógelo y guárdalo.

tr.en: Convince yourself that it is just as I write:
tr.it: Convinciti che è proprio come ti scrivo:
tr.es: Convéncete de que es tal como te escribo:

tr.en: some of our time is snatched from us, some is filched, some trickles away.
tr.it: certi momenti ci vengono strappati, altri sottratti, altri scivolano via.
tr.es: una parte del tiempo nos la arrebatan, otra nos la sustraen, otra se nos escurre.

tr.en: Yet the most shameful loss is the one that comes through carelessness.
tr.it: Ma la perdita più vergognosa è quella che avviene per negligenza.
tr.es: Pero la pérdida más vergonzosa es la que se produce por negligencia.

tr.en: And if you care to pay attention, a great part of life slips away from those who do wrong,
tr.it: E se vorrai farci caso, gran parte della vita sfugge a chi agisce male,
tr.es: Y si quieres prestar atención, gran parte de la vida se les escapa a quienes obran mal,

tr.en: the greatest part from those who do nothing, the whole of life from those who do something else.
tr.it: la maggior parte a chi non fa nulla, tutta la vita a chi fa altro.
tr.es: la mayor parte a quienes no hacen nada, la vida entera a quienes hacen otra cosa.

tr.en: Whom can you show me who puts any value on time, who knows what a day is worth,
tr.it: Chi mi mostrerai che dia un qualche valore al tempo, che sappia apprezzare un giorno,
tr.es: ¿A quién me mostrarás que dé algún valor al tiempo, que sepa estimar un día,

tr.en: who understands that he is dying every day?
tr.it: che capisca di morire ogni giorno?
tr.es: que comprenda que muere cada día?

tr.en: For this is where we are mistaken: we look ahead to death,
tr.it: In questo infatti ci inganniamo: vediamo la morte davanti a noi,
tr.es: En esto, en efecto, nos engañamos: vemos la muerte por delante,

tr.en: but a great part of it has already gone by; whatever of our life lies behind us, death holds.
tr.it: ma gran parte di essa è già passata: tutta la vita che ci sta alle spalle la possiede la morte.
tr.es: pero gran parte de ella ya ha pasado: toda la vida que queda atrás la tiene la muerte.

tr.en: So do, my dear Lucilius, what you write that you are doing: embrace every hour;
tr.it: Fa' dunque, mio Lucilio, quello che mi scrivi di fare: abbraccia tutte le ore;
tr.es: Haz, pues, querido Lucilio, lo que me escribes que haces: abraza todas las horas;

tr.en: so you will depend less on tomorrow, if you lay hold of today.
tr.it: così dipenderai meno dal domani, se metterai le mani sull'oggi.
tr.es: así dependerás menos del mañana, si echas mano del hoy.

tr.en: While it is being put off, life runs past.
tr.it: Mentre la si rinvia, la vita trascorre.
tr.es: Mientras se aplaza, la vida pasa corriendo.

tr.en: Everything, Lucilius, belongs to others; time alone is ours.
tr.it: Tutto, Lucilio, appartiene ad altri; solo il tempo è nostro.
tr.es: Todo, Lucilio, es ajeno; solo el tiempo es nuestro.

notes.n: vindicā tē tibi is a legal metaphor: vindicāre was to claim a thing—or a person, as when a slave was declared free—as one's own in court. 'Set yourself free, and keep yourself for yourself.' mī is the vocative of meus, Lūcīlī the vocative of Lūcīlius.

Three imperfects (auferēbātur, subripiēbātur, excidēbat) describe what kept happening to his time; two imperatives (collige, servā) give the remedy. colligō 'gather' → Italian cogliere, Spanish coger; servāre → Italian serbare, conservare.

quaedam … quaedam … quaedam 'some … others … others'. The three verbs grade the loss: ēripiuntur 'are snatched' (by force), subdūcuntur 'are filched' (by stealth), effluunt 'flow away' (by themselves).
iactūra is literally 'throwing overboard' (iaciō), hence 'loss, sacrifice'. neglegentia → Italian negligenza, Spanish negligencia.

volueris is future perfect, a polite 'if you will (care to)'. agentibus is a present participle in the dative, 'from people doing': male agentibus 'those doing wrong', nihil agentibus 'doing nothing', aliud agentibus 'doing something else'—a rising series magna, maxima, tōta.
pōnat, aestimet, intellegat are subjunctives in relative clauses of characteristic: 'the kind of man who…'. pretium → Italian prezzo, Spanish precio, French prix.
morī is the present infinitive of the deponent morior 'die' → Italian morire, Spanish morir, French mourir.
quidquid aetātis 'whatever (of) life-time': partitive genitive with quidquid. retrō 'behind' → Italian retro; French derrière comes from dē retrō.

quod facere tē scrībis 'what you write that you are doing' (accusative + infinitive). complectere is the imperative of the deponent complector 'embrace'. hōra → Italian ora, Spanish hora, French heure.

sīc fīet ut … pendeās 'so it will come about that you hang less on…': ut + subjunctive after fīō. crāstinum 'tomorrow' and hodiernum 'today' are neuter adjectives used as nouns. hodiē 'today' survives in Italian oggi, Spanish hoy and inside French aujourd'hui ('on the day of today').
vīta is the subject of both verbs: 'while (life) is being put off, life runs by'. differō 'carry apart, put off' → defer.
aliēna 'belonging to others' → Spanish ajeno, English alien. tantum here means 'only'.

title: I Hate and I Love; Hail and Farewell
author: Catullus
intro: Two of Catullus's most famous poems in elegiac couplets. Poem 85 compresses a whole tormented love affair into one couplet built on eight verbs. Poem 101 was written at the grave of his brother, who had died far from home near Troy, at the end of a long voyage; its closing 'hail and farewell' has been echoed by poets from Tennyson to Swinburne.

tr.en: I hate and I love. Why I do this, perhaps you ask.
tr.it: Odio e amo. Perché lo faccia, forse mi chiedi.
tr.es: Odio y amo. Por qué lo hago, quizá preguntes.

tr.en: I don't know, but I feel it happening, and I am in torment.
tr.it: Non lo so, ma sento che accade, e ne sono straziato.
tr.es: No lo sé, pero siento que sucede, y me siento torturado.

w: perf. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. m.
