notes.n: Chaerephon was Socrates' devoted and excitable friend, mocked in Aristophanes' Clouds. ἴστε: 2nd plural of οἶδα 'I know', a perfect with present meaning ('I have seen'), from the root ϝιδ- of Latin videō and English wit. Modern Greek has replaced it with ξέρω (from ἐξεύρω 'find out').
ἐκ νέου 'from youth'. ὑμῶν τῷ πλήθει 'to your majority', i.e. the democrats: Socrates reminds the jury that Chaerephon was on their side. πλῆθος 'multitude' → plethora; Modern πλήθος 'crowd'.

τὴν φυγὴν ταύτην: the democrats' exile under the Thirty Tyrants (404–403 BC). κατέρχομαι 'come down, come back' is the regular verb for an exile's return. φυγή 'flight, exile' → Modern φυγή 'escape', from φεύγω 'flee' (Modern φεύγω 'leave').

ἐφ’ ὅτι ὁρμήσειεν: an indefinite clause in past time takes the optative, 'whatever he rushed at'. ὁρμάω 'set in motion, rush' → hormone (a substance that 'sets going'); Modern ορμή 'impulse', ορμητικός 'impetuous'.
μαντεύσασθαι 'to consult the oracle', from μάντις 'seer' → English -mancy (necromancy); Modern μαντεύω means 'guess'. Δελφοί, the town and its inhabitants, is plural.
μὴ θορυβεῖτε: μή + present imperative, 'stop making a din' — the jury is already muttering. θόρυβος 'uproar' → Modern θόρυβος 'noise'.
ἤρετο: aorist of ἔρομαι 'ask', which supplies the aorist of ἐρωτάω (Modern ερώτηση 'question'). εἴη: optative in an indirect question after a past verb. ἐμοῦ: genitive of comparison, 'than me'.
ἀνεῖλεν: ἀναιρέω 'take up', the technical verb for an oracle 'giving its response' (as if drawing a lot). The Pythia was Apollo's priestess at Delphi, whose old name was Πυθώ.

τούτων πέρι: the preposition follows its noun (anastrophe) and its accent shifts back. οὑτοσί: οὗτος with the deictic -ί, 'this man here', as Socrates points to him in court. τετελεύτηκεν: perfect of τελευτάω 'end, die'.
διαβολή 'slander' (διαβάλλω 'throw across, accuse falsely'): its agent noun διάβολος 'slanderer' became the Devil — Latin diabolus, Italian diavolo, French diable; Modern διάβολος.
οὑτωσί: οὕτως + deictic -ί, 'like this'. ἐνεθυμούμην: imperfect of ἐνθυμέομαι 'take to heart, ponder' (θυμός 'spirit'); Modern ενθυμούμαι 'remember', ενθύμιο 'souvenir'.
τί ποτε 'what ever?' — ποτε adds impatience to a question. αἰνίττεται 'speaks in riddles', from αἶνος 'fable' and αἴνιγμα 'riddle' → enigma; Modern αίνιγμα.

σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ σοφὸς ὤν 'I am aware (lit. know with myself) that I am wise' — with οὔτε … οὔτε, 'I know I am not wise at all'. The same compound gives συνείδησις, Modern συνείδηση 'conscience', exactly like Latin cōnscientia (con- + scīre). σμικρός is the older Attic form of μικρός.
θέμις 'what is divinely right', also the goddess Themis. οὐ θέμις 'it is not permitted'. ψεύδομαι 'lie' → pseudo-; Modern ψέμα 'lie'.

title: The Political Animal
author: Aristotle
intro: In the second chapter of the Politics Aristotle traces the city (πόλις) from its roots in the household and the village and concludes that it exists by nature. Human beings are 'political animals' because nature has given them λόγος — speech and reason — with which to share ideas of right and wrong. Anyone who can live without a city, he says, must be either a beast or a god.

tr.en: From this, then, it is clear that the city belongs among the things that exist by nature,
tr.el: Από αυτά λοιπόν είναι φανερό ότι η πόλη ανήκει σε όσα υπάρχουν από τη φύση,

tr.en: and that man is by nature a political animal,
tr.el: και ότι ο άνθρωπος είναι από τη φύση του ζώο πολιτικό,

tr.en: and that one who is without a city by nature and not by chance
tr.el: και ότι όποιος ζει χωρίς πόλη εκ φύσεως και όχι από τύχη

tr.en: is either a poor sort of creature or something higher than a man.
tr.el: είναι είτε ένα ποταπό ον είτε κάτι ανώτερο από άνθρωπο.

tr.en: Why man is a political animal more than any bee or any herd animal is clear.
tr.el: Και γιατί ο άνθρωπος είναι πολιτικό ζώο περισσότερο από κάθε μέλισσα και κάθε αγελαίο ζώο, είναι φανερό.

tr.en: For nature, as we say, does nothing in vain;
tr.el: Γιατί η φύση, όπως λέμε, τίποτα δεν κάνει μάταια·

tr.en: and man alone among the animals has speech.
tr.el: και μόνο ο άνθρωπος από τα ζώα έχει λόγο.

tr.en: Voice, to be sure, is a sign of what is painful and pleasant,
tr.el: Η φωνή βέβαια είναι σημάδι του λυπηρού και του ευχάριστου,

tr.en: and so the other animals have it too;
tr.el: γι’ αυτό την έχουν και τα άλλα ζώα·

w: pres. act. ptcp. acc. sg. n.

tr.en: but speech exists to make clear what is beneficial and what is harmful,
tr.el: ο λόγος όμως υπάρχει για να φανερώνει το συμφέρον και το βλαβερό,

tr.en: and therefore also what is just and unjust.
tr.el: και επομένως και το δίκαιο και το άδικο.

tr.en: For this is what is peculiar to human beings, compared with the other animals:
tr.el: Γιατί αυτό είναι το ιδιαίτερο γνώρισμα των ανθρώπων σε σύγκριση με τα άλλα ζώα,

tr.en: they alone have a sense of good and bad, of just and unjust and the rest;
tr.el: ότι μόνο αυτοί έχουν αντίληψη του καλού και του κακού, του δίκαιου και του άδικου και των άλλων·

tr.en: and it is sharing in these things that makes a household and a city.
tr.el: και η κοινωνία σ’ αυτά δημιουργεί το νοικοκυριό και την πόλη.

w: pres. mid. ptcp. nom. sg. m.
pres. mid. ptcp. nom. sg. m.

tr.en: But whoever cannot live in partnership, or needs nothing because he is self-sufficient, is no part of a city,
tr.el: Όποιος όμως δεν μπορεί να ζει σε κοινωνία ή δεν έχει ανάγκη από τίποτα επειδή είναι αυτάρκης, δεν αποτελεί μέρος της πόλης,

tr.en: so that he is either a beast or a god.
tr.el: ώστε είναι είτε θηρίο είτε θεός.

notes.n: τῶν φύσει (ὄντων): partitive genitive, '(one) of the things that exist by nature'. φύσις 'nature', from φύω 'grow' → physics, physician; Modern φύση. πόλις → politics, metropolis; Modern πόλη.

πολιτικὸν ζῷον: 'a creature of the πόλις', made to live in a city-community — not 'political' in the modern sense of party politics. ζῷον 'living being' → zoo, zoology; Modern ζώο. Latin rendered the phrase animal sociāle or animal polīticum.
ἄπολις 'cityless', with the privative ἀ- ('un-', cognate with Latin in- and English un-) + πόλις. Aristotle goes on to quote Homer's curse on the man 'without clan, without law, without hearth'.

ἤτοι … ἤ 'either … or'. κρείττων 'stronger, better', used as a comparative of ἀγαθός (Ionic κρέσσων; Modern κρείττων 'superior', formal). φαῦλος 'mean, worthless'; Modern φαύλος 'vicious', as in φαύλος κύκλος 'vicious circle'.
μελίττης: Attic ττ (Ionic and Modern μέλισσα); the name Melissa means 'bee'. ἀγελαῖος 'living in herds' (ἀγέλη 'herd'); Modern αγελαίος has come to mean 'vulgar, common'.

οὐθέν: the later Attic spelling of οὐδέν. 'Nature does nothing in vain' is a guiding principle of Aristotle's biology (Latin nātūra nihil frūstrā facit). μάτην 'in vain' → Modern μάταια, μάταιος 'futile'.
λόγος means both 'speech' and 'reason'; Latin needed two words for it, ōrātiō and ratiō. It gives English logic and every -logy; Modern λόγος 'word, speech, reason'. μόνον 'alone' is an adverb here.
φωνή 'voice, sound' → phonetics, telephone; Modern φωνή. λυπηρός 'painful' (λύπη 'grief'; Modern λύπη 'sadness'). ἡδέος, genitive of ἡδύς 'sweet, pleasant' — ἡδονή 'pleasure' → hedonism.
Aristotle adds a parenthesis here (omitted): animals have come only as far as perceiving pain and pleasure and signalling them to one another. ὑπάρχω + dative 'belong to'; Modern υπάρχω 'exist'.

ἐπὶ τῷ δηλοῦν: articular infinitive, 'for the purpose of making clear' (δηλόω, Modern δηλώνω 'declare'). τὸ συμφέρον 'the advantageous' → Modern συμφέρον 'interest'; βλαβερός 'harmful' (βλάβη 'damage'; Modern βλάβη 'breakdown').
τὸ … ἔχειν: articular infinitive, explaining τοῦτο: 'namely, having perception …'. αἴσθησις 'perception' → aesthetics, anaesthesia; Modern αίσθηση 'feeling'.
κοινωνία 'partnership, community' → Modern κοινωνία 'society'. οἰκία here is the 'household', the first community, before the village (κώμη) and the city.
This sentence comes a few lines later in the chapter (1253a27–29). δεόμενος 'needing' (δέομαι + gen.). αὐτάρκεια 'self-sufficiency' (αὐτός + ἀρκέω 'suffice') → autarky; Modern αυτάρκεια.
θηρίον 'wild beast', diminutive of θήρ, which is cognate with Latin ferus 'wild' → feral, fierce; Modern θηρίο.

title: The Unexamined Life
orig: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ
author: Plato
intro: Socrates has been found guilty, and the jury must now choose his penalty. Why not simply go into exile and keep quiet? Socrates answers that he cannot: to stop questioning would be to disobey the god, and philosophical examination is the greatest good a human being can have. The passage contains the most famous sentence Plato ever wrote: 'the unexamined life is not worth living'.

tr.en: Perhaps, then, someone might say:
tr.el: Ίσως λοιπόν κάποιος θα έλεγε·

w: pres. act. ptcp. nom. sg. m.
pres. act. ptcp. nom. sg. m.
aor. act. ptcp. nom. sg. m.

tr.en: 'Socrates, can you not leave us and live in silence, keeping quiet?'
tr.el: «Σωκράτη, δεν θα μπορέσεις να φύγεις από κοντά μας και να ζεις σιωπηλός και ήσυχος;»

tr.en: This is the hardest thing of all to persuade some of you of.
tr.el: Αυτό ακριβώς είναι το πιο δύσκολο απ’ όλα, να πείσω μερικούς από εσάς.

tr.en: For if I say that this would mean disobeying the god,
tr.el: Γιατί αν πω ότι αυτό σημαίνει να παρακούσω τον θεό,

w: pres. mid. ptcp. dat. sg. m.

tr.en: and that for this reason I cannot keep quiet, you will not believe me, thinking I am being ironic;
tr.el: και ότι γι’ αυτό μου είναι αδύνατο να μείνω ήσυχος, δεν θα με πιστέψετε, νομίζοντας ότι ειρωνεύομαι·

tr.en: and if, on the other hand, I say that this is in fact the greatest good for a human being —
tr.el: κι αν πάλι πω ότι αυτό είναι πράγματι το μεγαλύτερο αγαθό για τον άνθρωπο,

tr.en: to discuss virtue every day
tr.el: να συζητά κάθε μέρα για την αρετή

w: pres. mid. ptcp. gen. sg. m.

tr.en: and the other things you hear me talking about
tr.el: και για τα άλλα, για τα οποία με ακούτε να συζητώ

w: pres. act. ptcp. gen. sg. m.

tr.en: as I examine both myself and others,
tr.el: εξετάζοντας και τον εαυτό μου και τους άλλους,

tr.en: and that the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being,
tr.el: και ότι η ζωή χωρίς αυτοεξέταση δεν αξίζει να τη ζει ο άνθρωπος,

w: pres. act. ptcp. dat. sg. m.

tr.en: you will believe me even less when I say these things.
tr.el: αυτά θα τα πιστέψετε ακόμη λιγότερο όταν σας τα λέω.

tr.en: Yet that is how things are, gentlemen, just as I say;
tr.el: Κι όμως έτσι έχουν τα πράγματα, όπως τα λέω, άνδρες·

tr.en: but it is not easy to convince you.
tr.el: μόνο που δεν είναι εύκολο να σας πείσω.

notes.n: ἄν + optative (εἴποι, aorist optative of the verb 'say') is the potential optative: 'someone might say'. Modern Greek expresses this with the conditional θα + past: κάποιος θα έλεγε.
οἷός τ’ ἔσῃ 'will you be able': οἷός τέ εἰμι + infinitive means 'I am able'. ἔσῃ is the 2nd singular future of εἰμί. ἡσυχία 'quiet' → Modern ησυχία, ήσυχος; ζῆν 'to live' (ζάω) → Modern ζω.
τουτί: τοῦτο with the deictic -ί, 'this, right here'; it is explained by the infinitive πεῖσαι 'to persuade'. χαλεπώτατον, superlative of χαλεπός 'difficult' (Modern χαλεπός 'hard, harsh', formal).
ἐάντε … ἐάντ’ (αὖ) 'whether … or (again)': ἐάν + subjunctive. λέγω here is the subjunctive, which looks the same as the indicative in the 1st singular. ἀπειθεῖν 'disobey' (ἀ- + πείθομαι 'obey').
πείσεσθε: future of πείθομαι 'obey, believe' (πείθω in the middle). εἰρωνευομένῳ 'feigning ignorance, dissembling': Socrates' famous εἰρωνεία became Latin īrōnīa and English irony; Modern ειρωνεία.

τοὺς λόγους ποιεῖσθαι 'to hold discussions'. ἀρετή 'excellence, virtue' → Modern αρετή. ἑκάστης ἡμέρας: genitive of time within which, 'every day' (ἡμέρα → ephemeral, ἐφήμερος 'lasting a day'; Modern ημέρα, μέρα).
ἐμοῦ … διαλεγομένου: genitive with ἀκούω, 'hear me conversing'. διαλέγομαι 'converse' → dialogue (διάλογος), dialect (διάλεκτος); Modern διάλογος, διάλεκτος.

The most quoted sentence of the Apology. ἀνεξέταστος 'unexamined' (ἀν- 'un-' + ἐξετάζω 'examine' → Modern εξετάσεις 'exams'). βιωτός 'livable' is the verbal adjective of βιόω 'live'. βίος 'life, way of life' → biography, biology; Modern βίος.
ἧττον 'less', comparative adverb from ἥττων 'inferior' (Attic ττ; Ionic ἧσσον). Modern ήττα 'defeat' comes from the same root.

ῥᾴδιον (ἐστί) 'it is easy': the neuter adjective with an infinitive is a common impersonal construction. Modern Greek says εύκολο, but ῥᾴδιος survives in ραδιουργία 'scheming', literally 'doing things too easily'.

title: The Wrath of Achilles
author: Homer
intro: The opening of the Iliad, Homer's epic of the Trojan War. In seven lines the poet calls on the Muse and names his theme: not the whole war, but the wrath of Achilles and the deaths it caused. These are the first lines of European literature, learned by heart by Greek schoolchildren for over two thousand years.

tr.en: Sing, goddess, of the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus,
tr.el: Την οργή τραγούδησε, θεά, του Αχιλλέα, του γιου του Πηλέα,

tr.en: that accursed wrath, which laid countless sorrows on the Achaeans,
tr.el: την ολέθρια, που φόρτωσε αμέτρητους πόνους στους Αχαιούς,

tr.en: and hurled down to Hades many mighty souls
tr.el: κι έστειλε στον Άδη πολλές γενναίες ψυχές

tr.en: of heroes, and made the men themselves a prey for dogs
tr.el: ηρώων, και τους ίδιους τους έκανε λεία για τα σκυλιά

tr.en: and for all the birds, and the will of Zeus was being fulfilled,
tr.el: και για όλα τα όρνια, κι η βουλή του Δία εκπληρωνόταν,

w: aor. act. ptcp. nom. du. m.

tr.en: from the moment when the two first parted in strife,
tr.el: από τη στιγμή που πρωτοχωρίστηκαν μαλώνοντας

tr.en: the son of Atreus, lord of men, and godlike Achilles.
tr.el: ο γιος του Ατρέα, ο άρχοντας των ανδρών, κι ο θεϊκός Αχιλλέας.

notes.n: μῆνιν, the first word of the poem, is the anger of a god or hero, more than ordinary ὀργή. ἄειδε is the uncontracted epic form of ᾄδω 'sing' (Attic ᾆδε); from the same root come ᾠδή → ode and Modern ωδή, τραγούδι (from τραγῳδία).

Πηληϊάδεω 'of the son of Peleus' is a patronymic (Πηληϊάδης) with the Homeric genitive -εω for Attic -ου, pronounced as one syllable. Ἀχιλῆος is the Homeric genitive of Ἀχιλλεύς (Attic Ἀχιλλέως); Homer writes one or two λ as the metre needs.

οὐλομένην 'accursed, ruinous' is an old aorist participle of ὄλλυμι 'destroy' used as an adjective. μυρί’ and ἄλγε’ are elided μυρία, ἄλγεα. μυρίος 'countless' → myriad; ἄλγος 'pain' → analgesic, neuralgia, Modern άλγος.

Ἄϊδι: dative of the Homeric name Ἄϊς (Attic Ἅιδης), 'to Hades', with no preposition. ἰφθίμους is feminine despite its -ους ending: in Homer many adjectives have only two endings. ψυχή, the breath of life that leaves the body at death → psyche, psychology; Modern ψυχή 'soul'.

τεῦχε: imperfect without the augment (Attic ἔτευχε), very common in Homer. κύνεσσιν: Homeric dative plural in -εσσι(ν) of κύων 'dog' (Attic κυσί); cognate with Latin canis and English hound → cynic, 'dog-like'.

οἰωνός is a large bird of prey; because birds were read as signs, Modern οιωνός means 'omen'. ἐτελείετο is from the epic by-form τελείω = τελέω 'fulfil' (τέλος 'end'; Modern τελειώνω 'finish'). Διός, genitive of Ζεύς: the stem Δι- is related to Latin Iuppiter, diēs and deus.

διαστήτην and ἐρίσαντε are duals: the two quarrelling heroes form a pair. διαστήτην is the 3rd person dual of the root aorist ἔστην 'stood' with διά 'apart'; ἐρίσαντε is from ἐρίζω 'quarrel', from ἔρις 'strife' (the goddess Eris; Modern έριδα).
Ἀτρεΐδης 'son of Atreus' is Agamemnon; ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν 'lord of men' is his standing epithet. δῖος 'godlike, shining' belongs with Ζεύς/Διός and Latin dīvus 'divine'.

title: At the coffee house
intro: The καφενείο, the traditional village or neighbourhood coffee house, is where Greek men have long met to drink coffee, read the paper, argue about politics and play backgammon. Mr Kostas orders his usual from Giannis, the owner, and waits for his backgammon partner Manolis.

tr.en: Good morning, Mr Kostas! What will you have today?
Good morning, Giannis. A Greek coffee, medium sweet, please.
And a glass of water, as always?
Yes, of course. Has Manolis come? I want to play backgammon.
Not yet. He always comes at ten.
Then I'll read the paper for a bit. What's in it today?
The same as ever, Mr Kostas: politics, football and the weather.
Here's your coffee. Enjoy!
Thanks. Ah, here's Manolis! Come, sit here.
Good morning, everyone! Giannis, a coffee for me too — no sugar.
Right away! And who's going to win at backgammon today?
Me, of course! Manolis only wins in his dreams.
We'll see, my friend, we'll see!

notes.n: Giannis uses the polite plural (θα πάρετε 'you (pl.) will take') to an older customer. κύριε is the vocative of κύριος 'lord, Mr' — the same form as in the church's Κύριε ελέησον 'Lord, have mercy'. Names in -ας lose their -ς in the vocative: Κώστας → Κώστα, Γιάννης → Γιάννη.

A Greek coffee is ordered by sweetness: σκέτος 'plain' (no sugar), μέτριος 'medium', γλυκός 'sweet'. μέτριος is Ancient μέτριος 'moderate' (μέτρον 'measure'); σκέτος is Italian schietto 'pure, unmixed'.
τάβλι 'backgammon' comes, through Byzantine τάβλιον, from Latin tabula 'board' — the source of English table. Ήρθε 'he came' is the aorist of έρχομαι (Ancient ἔρχομαι, aorist ἦλθον → ήλθα → ήρθα).
εφημερίδα 'newspaper' is Ancient ἐφημερίς 'daily record' (ἐπί + ἡμέρα 'day'), the family of English ephemeral.
πολιτική is from πολιτικός 'of the citizens' (πόλις 'city'), like English politics. ποδόσφαιρο is a modern compound of πόδι 'foot' and σφαίρα 'ball' — a calque of English football.
σας 'your' is the weak form of εσείς; possessive pronouns follow the noun: ο καφές σας 'your coffee'.
Έλα 'come!' is the irregular imperative of έρχομαι, ultimately from the Ancient aorist imperative ἐλθέ. κάθισε 'sit!' belongs to κάθομαι, from Ancient κάθημαι/καθίζω.
για μένα 'for me': after prepositions Greek uses the strong pronoun (εμένα, shortened to μένα). σκέτο agrees with the masculine καφέ.
όνειρο 'dream' is Ancient ὄνειρος/ὄνειρον (cf. oneiromancy). Note the extra accent in όνειρά του: a word stressed on the third syllable from the end gets a second accent when a weak pronoun follows.

title: At the street market
intro: Every neighbourhood in a Greek town has its λαϊκή (αγορά), a street market held on the same weekday each week, where farmers sell fruit and vegetables straight from their fields. Mrs Lena does her shopping at Stelios's stall. Notice the polite plural imperatives (δώστε, βάλτε) and the prices.

tr.en: Come on, ladies! Fresh tomatoes, sweet melons, whatever you want!
Good morning. How much are the tomatoes?
One euro fifty a kilo. They're from Crete — look!
Give me two kilos, please. And a bunch of parsley.
Right away. Would you like some cucumbers too? I picked them this morning.
Yes, two cucumbers. Are the oranges sweet?
Like honey! Try one, madam.
Indeed, it's very juicy! Put in three kilos for me.
Here you are. Anything else?
No, thank you. How much is it all together?
Ten euros. And the parsley is a present!
Thank you so much! Good luck with your work.
Have a good day! And next Wednesday, here again!

notes.n: λαϊκός 'of the people' comes from λαός 'people' — the same word that reached English through Latin laicus as lay and laity. αγορά is the Ancient agora, the market square; from it come αγοράζω 'buy' and English agoraphobia. ντομάτα is from Italian (Venetian) tomata, ultimately from Nahuatl tomatl; πεπόνι is Ancient πέπων 'ripe (melon)', the source, through Latin pepo and French, of English pumpkin.
Πόσο κάνει/κάνουν; 'how much does it/do they cost?' — literally 'how much does it make?'

Δώστε 'give!' is the polite (plural) imperative of δίνω, the modern form of Ancient δίδωμι. μάτσο 'bunch' is Italian mazzo. μαϊντανός 'parsley' made a round trip: Turkish maydanoz comes from Byzantine Greek μακεδονήσι 'Macedonian (parsley)' and came back into Greek in its Turkish shape.
Τα έκοψα 'I cut (picked) them': the weak object pronoun goes before the verb. κόβω is Ancient κόπτω 'cut'.
πορτοκάλι 'orange' is named after Portugal (Italian portogallo), because sweet oranges reached the Mediterranean through Portuguese traders.
μέλι 'honey' has not changed since Homer; Latin mel (Italian miele, French miel) is a cognate.
Βάλτε μου 'put (in) for me' — the aorist imperative of βάζω. ζουμερός 'juicy' comes from ζουμί 'juice', Byzantine ζωμίον, from Ancient ζωμός 'broth'.
Να ’στε καλά 'may you be well' (να είστε καλά, with the vowel elided) is the warm everyday way of saying thank you.
Τετάρτη 'Wednesday' is simply 'the fourth (day)'; Δευτέρα, Τρίτη and Πέμπτη are likewise numbers, while Παρασκευή is 'preparation' (for the Sabbath).

title: Meeting someone
intro: Eleni, who lives in Athens, meets Marco, an Italian student. The dialogue practises the first phrases everyone needs: names, where you come from, what you do. Along the way the two discover how many words Greek and Italian share — in both directions.

tr.en: Hi! My name is Eleni. What's your name?
Hi, Eleni! My name is Marco. Pleased to meet you.
Me too. Where are you from, Marco?
I'm from Italy, from Rome. Are you from Athens?
No, I'm from Thessaloniki, but now I live here. What are you doing in Athens?
I'm studying history at the university. I'm learning Greek too.
You speak Greek very well!
Thank you! I speak a little, but I'm trying.
Lots of Greek words exist in Italian too, like "theatre" (teatro) and "music" (musica).
And in Greek you have lots of Italian words: "porta", "fresco", "bravo"!
Well done you! Shall we go for a coffee?
Yes, gladly! Let's go.

notes.n: Με λένε Ελένη is literally 'they call me Eleni': λέω 'say, call' (Ancient λέγω) with the weak pronoun με 'me'. To a stranger you would ask politely: Πώς σας λένε; Note the Greek question mark (;), which looks like an English semicolon.
Χαίρω πολύ 'I rejoice greatly' = 'pleased to meet you'. χαίρω is the Ancient verb unchanged; its imperative χαῖρε 'rejoice!' was the everyday Greek greeting, the counterpart of Latin avē.
Κι is the form of και used before a vowel. πού with an accent asks 'where?'; που without it is the relative 'who, which, where'.
σπουδάζω 'study' is Ancient σπουδάζω 'be eager, busy oneself' (σπουδή 'zeal'). ιστορία is Ancient ἱστορία 'inquiry', which Latin borrowed as historia → Italian storia, English history and story.

ελληνικά 'Greek (the language)' is the neuter plural of ελληνικός: μιλάω ελληνικά, ιταλικά, αγγλικά. μιλάω is Ancient ὁμιλέω 'converse' (cf. homily) with its first vowel worn away: ὁμιλῶ → ομιλώ → μιλώ/μιλάω.

θέατρο (θέατρον 'a place for watching', from θεάομαι 'watch') and μουσική (ἡ μουσικὴ τέχνη 'the art of the Muses') went into Latin as theatrum and musica, and from there into Italian, Spanish, French and English.

Words also travelled the other way. πόρτα is Italian/Venetian porta (Latin porta); it replaced Ancient θύρα, which survives only in learned words such as θυρωρός 'doorman'. φρέσκος is Italian fresco, μπράβο is bravo — Greek writes the b-sound as μπ.
καφές comes from Turkish kahve (from Arabic qahwa); Greek added a masculine -ς. Italian caffè and English coffee go back to the same Arabic word. The masculine accusative έναν keeps its final -ν.
Πάμε 'let's go' is simply the 1st plural of πάω 'go', used as an invitation. πάω is a worn-down form of Ancient ὑπάγω 'go away' (ὑπάγω → πάγω → πάω).

title: My family
intro: Sofia, a fifteen-year-old from Piraeus, introduces her family — from her father the sailor to her grandparents in a village in the Peloponnese. The text practises the present tense, family words and possessives (ο πατέρας μου 'my father').

tr.en: My name is Sofia and I am fifteen years old.
I live with my family in a flat in Piraeus.
My father is called Nikos and he is a sailor.
He travels a lot and brings us presents from all over the world.
My mother, Maria, is a teacher at a primary school.
I have an older brother, Giorgos, and a little sister, Eleni.
Giorgos is twenty and studies medicine in Thessaloniki.
Eleni is only six and plays all day with our cat.
My grandparents live in a village near Kalamata.
My grandmother cooks the tastiest food in the world.
My grandfather has a plot of land with olive trees and makes his own oil.
Every summer we all go to the village together.
I love my family very much!

notes.n: Age is given with the genitive plural χρονών 'of years': είμαι δεκαπέντε χρονών. χρόνος 'time; year' is Ancient χρόνος, as in chronology and chronic.

οικογένεια 'family' is a learned compound of οἶκος 'house' and γένος 'kin'. In οικογένειά μου the noun takes a second accent because the weak pronoun μου follows a word stressed on the third syllable from the end.

πατέρας and μητέρα show a typical Modern Greek change: new nominatives were built on the Ancient accusatives πατέρα, μητέρα (from πατήρ, μήτηρ). λέγεται 'is called' is the passive of λέω. ναυτικός 'sailor' comes from ναύτης/ναῦς 'ship' — compare Latin nauta, English nautical.
δώρο 'gift' is Ancient δῶρον, familiar from names like Θεόδωρος 'gift of God' (Theodore, Dorothy).

δασκάλα is the feminine of δάσκαλος 'teacher', a shortening of Ancient διδάσκαλος (διδάσκω 'teach', cf. didactic). δημοτικό σχολείο 'primary school' is literally 'municipal school' (δῆμος 'people, district').
αδελφός/αδελφή go back to Ancient ἀδελφός 'from the same womb' (δελφύς) — compare Philadelphia 'brotherly love'. Colloquially you will also hear αδερφός.
ιατρική 'medicine' keeps the learned form of ιατρός; the everyday word for 'doctor' is γιατρός, the same word with its first syllable reshaped in speech.
παππούς 'grandfather' is Ancient πάππος; the plural παππούδες means 'grandparents' as well as 'grandfathers'. Kalamata is a town in the southern Peloponnese famous for its olives.
φαγητό 'food' is built on φαγεῖν, the Ancient aorist of 'eat' (ἐσθίω), the root also seen in sarcophagus 'flesh-eater' and -phage.
λάδι 'oil' (Byzantine λάδιον, from ἔλαιον) and ελιά 'olive' (ἐλαία) are Ancient words; Latin borrowed them as oleum and olīva, whence Italian olio, oliva and English oil, olive.
καλοκαίρι 'summer' is literally καλός καιρός 'fine weather'; the Ancient word θέρος survives only in learned words such as θερινός 'summery'.

title: A day in Athens
intro: A day's sightseeing in Athens: the Acropolis in the morning, lunch in the Plaka, the Acropolis Museum in the afternoon and the floodlit Parthenon at night. Many of the words are the names of buildings that have kept their Ancient Greek names for 2,500 years.

tr.en: In the morning we went up to the Acropolis very early, before the heat and the crowds.
We passed through the Propylaea and saw the Parthenon in front of us.
The temple was built in the fifth century BC for the goddess Athena.
The city took its name from her, as the myth tells.
Athena gave the Athenians an olive tree and defeated Poseidon.
Next to the Parthenon stands the Erechtheion with the famous Caryatids.
Then we went down to the Plaka, the oldest neighbourhood in Athens.
We walked through the narrow alleys, among neoclassical houses and Byzantine churches.
The shops were selling souvenirs, jewellery and sandals.
For lunch we sat down at a taverna with a view of the Acropolis.
In the afternoon we visited the Acropolis Museum.
In the evening, from Philopappos Hill, we saw the Parthenon lit up.
It was an unforgettable day!

notes.n: ακρόπολη is 'the top (ἄκρος) of the city (πόλις)' — every Ancient Greek city had one; compare acrobat and acronym. ανεβαίνω 'go up' is Ancient ἀναβαίνω, the verb behind Xenophon's Anabasis 'the march up-country'. τον κόσμο 'the crowds': κόσμος means both 'world' and 'people'.
Προπύλαια is 'what stands before (πρό) the gates (πύλη)'. Παρθενώνας is Ancient Παρθενών 'the hall of the Maiden' (παρθένος), i.e. of Athena Parthenos.
χτίστηκε 'was built' is the passive aorist of χτίζω (Ancient κτίζω). αιώνας 'century' is Ancient αἰών 'age' (English eon). ναός 'temple' is Ancient ναός/νεώς 'dwelling of a god'.
μύθος is Ancient μῦθος 'word, tale', English myth. In the contest for the city Poseidon struck the rock and produced a salt spring; Athena planted the first olive tree and won.
χαρίζω 'give as a present' is Ancient χαρίζομαι, from χάρις 'grace, favour' (charisma). νικάω is Ancient νικάω, from νίκη 'victory' — the goddess Nike.
The Caryatids, the maidens who hold up the porch of the Erechtheion, are said to be named after the women of Karyai in Laconia. περίφημος 'famous' is the Ancient περίφημος, from φήμη 'fame'.

σοκάκι 'alley' is Turkish sokak 'street'. εκκλησία 'church' is Ancient ἐκκλησία 'assembly'; borrowed into Latin as ecclesia, it gave Italian chiesa, Spanish iglesia, French église. The neoclassical houses date from the 19th century, after Athens became the capital of independent Greece.
σουβενίρ is French souvenir and, like most recent loanwords, is indeclinable. κόσμημα 'jewel' is from κοσμέω 'adorn' (κόσμος 'order, ornament' — compare cosmetic). σανδάλι is Ancient σανδάλιον.
ταβέρνα is Italian taverna, from Latin taberna 'hut, shop'. με θέα την Ακρόπολη 'with a view of the Acropolis' — θέα 'view' is the root of θέατρο.
μουσείο is Ancient μουσεῖον 'seat of the Muses', Latin museum. Time of day is expressed by the plain accusative: το απόγευμα 'in the afternoon', το βράδυ 'in the evening'.
φωτισμένο 'lit up' is the passive participle of φωτίζω, from φως 'light' (Ancient φῶς, φωτός — photo-).
αξέχαστος 'unforgettable' is ξεχνάω 'forget' with the privative prefix α- 'un-', which has been productive since Ancient Greek (ἀθάνατος 'immortal').

title: A letter from Crete
intro: Katerina writes to her friend Anna from her holidays in Chania, in western Crete. Crete's history is layered in its vocabulary: Minoan palaces and myths, four centuries of Venetian rule (1211–1669), then the Ottomans. The letter also shows the conventional openings and closings of a Greek letter.

tr.en: My dear Anna,
I'm writing to you from Chania, where I'm spending my holidays.
Crete is beautiful and the Cretans are very hospitable.
Wherever you go, they offer you raki!
The old harbour with its lighthouse and Venetian houses is like a painting.
Yesterday we went to Knossos and saw the palace of King Minos.
The guide told us the myth of Theseus and the Minotaur in the labyrinth.
Today we swam at Elafonisi, which has pink sand!
The food here is wonderful: dakos, graviera cheese, wild greens with olive oil and, of course, snails!
Every evening we listen to the lyra and the lute in the tavernas.
An old man sang me a mantinada about love and the sea.
I miss you very much! I'll bring you oil and honey from the village.
Lots of love,
your Katerina

notes.n: Letters open with Αγαπητέ/Αγαπητή 'dear' — Ancient ἀγαπητός 'beloved', from ἀγαπάω, the verb of Christian ἀγάπη 'love'.
διακοπές 'holidays' is the plural of διακοπή 'interruption' (διακόπτω 'cut through'): a break from work. Χανιά is a plural place name, so the article is τα.
Όπου κι αν πας 'wherever you go'. κερνάω 'treat (to a drink)' is Ancient κεράννυμι 'mix wine'. ρακή, the Cretan grape spirit, is Turkish rakı.

φάρος 'lighthouse' is named after Pharos, the island off Alexandria with the great lighthouse — hence Italian faro, French phare. λιμάνι 'harbour' is Byzantine λιμένιον, a diminutive of Ancient λιμήν. ενετικός 'Venetian' comes from Ενετοί, the Greek name of the Veneti.

Κνωσός, like many ancient place names in -ος, is feminine: η Κνωσός, στην Κνωσό. Μίνωας is a modern nominative built on the ancient accusative Μίνωα (of Μίνως). παλάτι is from Latin palatium, the Palatine Hill where the Roman emperors lived.

μάς carries an accent here to show it is the object of είπε ('told us'), not 'our' with ξεναγός ('our guide'). ξεναγός 'guide' is 'one who leads (ἄγω) strangers (ξένοι)'. λαβύρινθος is a pre-Greek word, sometimes linked with labrys, the Minoan double axe.
άμμος 'sand' is feminine, as in Ancient Greek (ἡ ἄμμος). Ελαφονήσι means 'deer island'.
γραβιέρα is Gruyère, borrowed through Italian groviera. χόρτα 'wild greens' is the plural of χόρτο, Ancient χόρτος 'pasture, fodder', a cognate of Latin hortus 'garden' and English garden/yard.
The Cretan λύρα is a bowed fiddle, but its name is the Ancient λύρα 'lyre'. λαούτο 'lute' is Italian liuto, which goes back (through Provençal) to Arabic al-ʿūd 'the oud'.

A μαντινάδα is an improvised rhyming couplet of fifteen syllables per line; the word is Venetian mattinada 'morning song, serenade'. τραγουδώ 'sing' is Ancient τραγῳδέω 'perform tragedy': τραγῳδία 'goat-song' became the ordinary word for song, τραγούδι.
Μου λείπεις 'I miss you' is literally 'you are lacking to me': the person missed is the subject, exactly as in French tu me manques and Italian mi manchi.
φιλί 'kiss' is from φιλώ 'kiss, love' (Ancient φιλέω). Letters end with Πολλά φιλιά or Φιλιά.

title: A trip to Thessaloniki
intro: A traveller describes a few days in Thessaloniki, Greece's second city: the seafront and the White Tower, the Upper Town, Roman and Byzantine monuments, and the food. The text practises the past tenses — the aorist for single events (πήγα, είδα) and the imperfect for repeated or ongoing ones (έβλεπα, έτρωγα).

tr.en: Last week I went by train from Athens to Thessaloniki.
The journey took four hours, and from the window I could see Mount Olympus.
Thessaloniki is the second largest city in Greece.
King Cassander founded it and gave it the name of his wife.
Thessalonike was the sister of Alexander the Great.
On the first morning I walked along the seafront as far as the White Tower.
Then I went up to the Upper Town, with its narrow little streets and old houses.
From there the view over the Thermaic Gulf was magical.
I also visited Hagia Sophia and the Rotunda, a Roman building of the emperor Galerius.
Every morning I ate bougatsa with custard, the city's best-known treat.
In the evening my friends took me to an ouzeri in Ladadika.
The people of Thessaloniki are hospitable and know how to enjoy themselves.
I definitely want to go back!

notes.n: περασμένη 'last' is literally 'passed', the participle of περνάω. εβδομάδα 'week' is Ancient ἑβδομάς 'a group of seven'. τρένο is Italian treno (from French train).

έβλεπα 'I was seeing' is the imperfect: a continuing view, not a single glance. Όλυμπος, the highest mountain in Greece, was the home of the Olympian gods. κρατάω 'last, hold' is Ancient κρατέω 'be strong, hold fast'.
The comparative μεγαλύτερος 'bigger' is a new formation from μεγάλος; Ancient Greek used the irregular μείζων. 'The second largest' is η δεύτερη μεγαλύτερη 'the second biggest'.
Cassander, one of Alexander's successors, founded the city in 315 BC. ιδρύω 'found' is Ancient ἱδρύω 'make to sit, establish' (related to ἕδρα 'seat', cf. cathedral).
The name Θεσσαλονίκη means 'victory (νίκη) over the Thessalians' — given to the princess by her father Philip II after a battle.

Λευκός 'white' is the learned, ancient word, used in names; everyday Greek says άσπρος, from Byzantine ἄσπρος, from Latin asper 'rough' — said of freshly minted, shining silver coins. πύργος 'tower' is Ancient πύργος.
Άνω 'upper' is the Ancient adverb ἄνω 'above', kept in place names. δρομάκι 'little street' is a diminutive of δρόμος, Ancient δρόμος 'running, race-course' (cf. hippodrome).
κόλπος 'gulf' is Ancient κόλπος 'bosom, fold; bay'. Through Latin colpus it became Italian golfo, French golfe and English gulf.

Αγία Σοφία means 'Holy Wisdom', not a saint called Sophia. The Rotunda is a round Roman building of about AD 300, later a church and then a mosque; ροτόντα comes from Latin rotunda 'round'. αυτοκράτορας 'emperor' is the Greek translation of Latin imperator.

μπουγάτσα, a filo pie with custard, cheese or mince, comes through Turkish poğaça from Italian focaccia (Latin focus 'hearth'). κρέμα is Italian crema / French crème. λιχουδιά 'delicacy' is from λείχω 'lick'.
Λαδάδικα, the old warehouse district by the port, is named after the oil (λάδι) merchants who once traded there. An ουζερί is a place serving ouzo with small dishes (μεζέδες).

φιλόξενος 'hospitable' is 'friend (φίλος) of strangers (ξένος)'. ξέρω 'know' is Byzantine ἐξεύρω 'find out', Ancient ἐξευρίσκω. διασκεδάζω 'have fun' is Ancient διασκεδάννυμι 'scatter' — one scatters one's cares.
The prefix ξανα- means 'again': ξαναπάω 'go again', ξαναλέω 'say again'. It comes from ἐξ + ἀνά.

title: At the restaurant
intro: Anna and Petros order dinner in a taverna. The Greek menu is a history lesson in itself: next to Ancient Greek words stand dishes and objects borrowed from Italian (from centuries of Venetian rule on the islands) and from Turkish (from the Ottoman centuries).

tr.en: Good evening! Are you ready to order?
Yes. For starters we'd like a village salad and tzatziki.
And a portion of meatballs, please.
Very good. And for the main course?
What do you recommend? Is the moussaka fresh?
Certainly — the cook made it this morning. We also have pastitsio.
I'll have a souvlaki with chips.
And I'll have the moussaka. And half a kilo of red wine, please.
House wine, from the barrel? It's very good.
Yes, great. And bring us some bread, please.
Everything was wonderful! Can we have the bill?
Right away. And the dessert is on the house!
Thank you very much! Have a good evening!

notes.n: εστιατόριο 'restaurant' is a 19th-century learned coinage from Ancient ἑστιάω 'entertain at one's hearth' (ἑστία 'hearth', the goddess Hestia — compare Latin Vesta). σερβιτόρος 'waiter' is Italian servitore 'servant'. παραγγέλνω 'order' is Ancient παραγγέλλω 'give orders'.
σαλάτα is Italian (in)salata, from sal 'salt'. τζατζίκι is Turkish cacık. ορεκτικό 'starter' is from όρεξη 'appetite', Ancient ὄρεξις 'desire' — hence the wish καλή όρεξη 'bon appétit'.
μερίδα 'portion' is Ancient μερίς (μέρος 'part'). κεφτές is Turkish köfte (from Persian kofta).
πιάτο 'plate, dish' is Italian piatto. κυρίως πιάτο 'main course': κυρίως 'mainly' is the adverb of κύριος 'principal'.
μουσακάς is Turkish musakka (from Arabic). Turkish nouns in -a usually became Greek masculines in -άς: μουσακάς, μεζές 'snack' (meze), καβγάς 'quarrel'.
παστίτσιο 'baked pasta pie' is Italian pasticcio 'pie; mess'. μάγειρας 'cook' is Ancient μάγειρος.
σουβλάκι 'little skewer' is the diminutive of σούβλα 'spit', from Latin subula 'awl'. πατάτα is Italian patata. τηγανητός 'fried' comes from τηγάνι 'frying pan', Ancient τήγανον.

κρασί 'wine' is Byzantine κρασίον, from κρᾶσις 'mixing' — the Greeks drank their wine mixed with water. It replaced Ancient οἶνος, which survives in learned words like οινοπωλείο 'wine shop' and is a cognate of Latin vīnum. In tavernas house wine is ordered by weight: μισό κιλό, ένα κιλό.
βαρέλι 'barrel' is Venetian barile. χύμα 'loose, unbottled' comes from χύνω 'pour' (Ancient χέω).
φέρτε 'bring!' is the polite imperative of φέρνω (Ancient φέρω, cognate with Latin ferō and English bear). ψωμί 'bread' is Byzantine ψωμίον 'morsel'; it replaced Ancient ἄρτος, still heard in church.
λογαριασμός 'bill' comes from λογαριάζω 'reckon', built on λόγος in its old sense of 'account, reckoning'.
κερνάω 'treat someone (to a drink)' is Ancient κεράννυμι 'mix (wine)'; κερασμένο 'treated' = on the house. μαγαζί 'shop' is Venetian magazen (Italian magazzino, from Arabic makhāzin 'storehouses').
Καλή συνέχεια! 'a good continuation!' is the standard wish when parting from someone in the middle of their day or evening.

title: Greek proverbs
intro: Fifteen proverbs and sayings still in everyday use. Some are pure folk speech full of Italian and Turkish words; others are Ancient Greek sentences that have been quoted for 2,500 years and keep their ancient grammar — datives, participles and all.

tr.en: One swallow does not bring the spring.
The beginning is half of the whole.
Slowly, slowly the sour grape turns into honey.
Better late than never.
A good captain shows himself in the storm.
The tongue has no bones, yet it breaks bones.
Where many roosters crow, dawn is slow to come.
Bean by bean the sack fills up.
The pear has its tail at the back.
Learn a trade and put it aside; if you go hungry, take it up.
A healthy mind in a healthy body.
What happens in the house should not be aired in public.
No evil comes unmixed with good.

w: pres. pass. ptcp. nom. sg. m. (ancient form)

tr.en: I grow old, always learning.
A good day shows itself from the morning.

notes.n: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.7: μία γὰρ χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ 'one swallow does not make spring'. Ancient χελιδών lives on as the diminutive χελιδόνι, while ἔαρ 'spring' gave way to άνοιξη. English turned the spring into a summer.

An ancient saying (ἀρχὴ ἥμισυ παντός) attributed to Pythagoras and quoted by Plato and Aristotle; Horace has dimidium factī quī coepit habet. ήμισυ 'half' and παντός 'of the whole' are learned forms — everyday Greek says μισό and όλου — but they live on in hemisphere and pantheon.

αγουρίδα 'sour, unripe grape' comes from άγουρος 'unripe', Ancient ἄωρος 'out of season' (ἀ- + ὥρα). σιγά 'slowly, quietly' was originally σιγῇ 'in silence'. The idea echoes σπεῦδε βραδέως 'hurry slowly', Augustus's motto, Latin festīnā lentē.
κάλλιο 'better' is κάλλιον, the neuter of the Ancient comparative καλλίων 'finer'. Livy has the Latin equivalent: potius sērō quam numquam.

The repeated article (ο καλός ο καπετάνιος) gives emphasis. Both nouns are Italian: καπετάνιος is Venetian capitanio (Latin caput 'head'), φουρτούνα is fortuna, which in Italian also means 'storm at sea'. φαίνομαι 'appear' is Ancient φαίνομαι (phenomenon).
γλώσσα is Ancient γλῶσσα 'tongue; language' (glossary). κόκαλο 'bone' is Byzantine κόκκαλον; Ancient ὀστοῦν survives only in learned words such as οστό and osteo-.

Too many cooks spoil the broth. λαλώ 'crow, chatter' is Ancient λαλέω 'talk' (glossolalia). ξημερώνει 'day breaks' is built on ημέρα: ἐξ + ἡμέρα. αργώ 'be late' is Ancient ἀργέω 'be idle', from ἀ-εργός 'not working'.

φασόλι/φασούλι 'bean' made a round trip: Ancient φάσηλος went into Latin as phaseolus (Italian fagiolo) and came back into Byzantine Greek as φασούλιον. σακούλι 'little sack' is a diminutive of σάκ(κ)ος, a Semitic word that passed through Greek into Latin saccus and English sack.
The hardest part is still to come. αχλάδα/αχλάδι 'pear' is Ancient ἀχράς, -άδος 'wild pear', with ρ turned to λ. ουρά 'tail' is Ancient οὐρά.

άσ’ την and πιάσ’ την are άσε την 'leave it', πιάσε την 'take it' with the final vowel elided. άσε is the short imperative of αφήνω 'let, leave', Ancient ἀφίημι. τέχνη 'craft, art' is the source of technique and technology.

Juvenal's mēns sāna in corpore sānō, put into learned Greek with the Ancient dative case (σώματι, υγιεί) after εν 'in'. The dative has vanished from spoken Greek; in everyday speech this would be υγιές μυαλό σε υγιές σώμα.
'Don't wash your dirty linen in public.' Datives again: εν οίκω 'in the house', εν δήμω 'among the people'. οἶκος gives economy and ecology, δῆμος gives democracy.

Every cloud has a silver lining. A katharevousa sentence: ουδέν 'nothing' (Ancient οὐδέν; everyday τίποτα), κακόν with its old final -ν, αμιγής 'unmixed' from ἀ- + μείγνυμι 'mix' (a cognate of Latin miscēre and English mix).

Solon, quoted by Plutarch: γηράσκω δ’ αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος 'I grow old, always learning many things'. γηράσκω gives geriatrics; διδασκόμενος is a present participle of a type that has vanished from the spoken language.
Compare English 'the morning shows the day'. μέρα is Ancient ἡμέρα with its unstressed first vowel lost; πρωί is Ancient πρωΐ 'early'.

title: Weather and seasons
intro: A short description of the Greek year, from the 'halcyon days' of January to the north winds of August. Note how time expressions use the accusative without a preposition: τον Ιανουάριο 'in January', το καλοκαίρι 'in summer'. The month names are Latin, but the seasons are Greek.

tr.en: Greece has a mild climate, with a lot of sun and little rain.
Winter is short, but in the mountains it often snows.
In January the "halcyon days" usually come, warm and calm.
In spring nature wakes up and flowers bloom everywhere.
In summer it is very hot and the sky is always deep blue.
In July and August the temperature often reaches forty degrees.
Then the meltemia blow, strong north winds over the Aegean.
People leave the city and go swimming on the islands.
In autumn the days grow shorter and the first rains come.
But in October "St Demetrius' little summer" often comes.
March is the most changeable month: one day sun, the next day rain.
That is why we say: "March the flayer, wicked burner of the vine-stakes."
And you — which season do you prefer?

notes.n: κλίμα is Ancient κλίμα 'slope' — the 'slope' of the earth towards the pole, hence a zone or region; Latin borrowed it as clima, English climate. ήπιος 'mild' is a Homeric word. ήλιος is Ancient ἥλιος (helium, heliocentric).

χειμώνας is a new nominative made from the Ancient accusative χειμῶνα (χειμών). βουνό 'mountain' comes from Ancient βουνός 'hill', a rare word that pushed out ὄρος in everyday speech. χιονίζει 'it snows' is from χιόνι 'snow' (Ancient χιών).

The 'halcyon days' are named after the myth of Alcyone, turned into a kingfisher (ἀλκυών): Zeus calms the winds in midwinter so that she can hatch her eggs on the sea. English 'halcyon days' comes from the same story.
άνοιξη 'spring' is literally 'opening' (Ancient ἄνοιξις, from ἀνοίγω 'open'); it replaced Ancient ἔαρ. ανθίζω 'bloom' comes from άνθος 'flower', as in anthology 'a gathering of flowers'.

κάνει ζέστη 'it is hot' — literally 'it makes heat' — like Italian fa caldo, Spanish hace calor, French il fait chaud. ζέστη comes from ζεστός, from Ancient ζέω 'boil'. καταγάλανος 'deep blue' adds the intensive prefix κατα- to γαλανός 'blue'.

The month names are Roman, borrowed through Byzantium: Ιούλιος (Julius Caesar), Αύγουστος (Augustus), Ιανουάριος (Janus). θερμοκρασία 'temperature' is a learned compound of θερμός 'warm' and κρᾶσις 'mixture' (cf. thermometer).
μελτέμι, the strong dry north wind of the Aegean summer, comes from Turkish meltem (itself of disputed origin). βοριάς 'north wind' is Βορέας, Boreas — compare English boreal.
μπάνιο 'bath, swim' made a round trip: Greek βαλανεῖον 'bath' → Latin balneum → Italian bagno → Greek μπάνιο.
φθινόπωρο 'autumn' is Ancient φθινόπωρον, 'the waning (φθίνω) of the fruit season (ὀπώρα)'.
Saint Demetrius, patron saint of Thessaloniki, is celebrated on 26 October, when a spell of warm weather often returns.
Μάρτιος is Latin Martius (the month of Mars). άστατος 'changeable' is Ancient ἄστατος 'unstable', from the root of ἵστημι 'stand'.

In this proverb Μάρτης is the popular form of Μάρτιος. γδάρτης 'flayer' comes from γδέρνω 'skin' (Ancient ἐκδέρω): the March cold strips you raw. A παλουκοκαύτης is a 'stake-burner' — by March the firewood runs out and people burn the vineyard stakes (παλούκι, ultimately from Latin pālus 'stake').
εποχή 'season, era' is Ancient ἐποχή 'pause, fixed point', an astronomers' term that also gave English epoch. Γι’ αυτό 'for that reason' is για with its final vowel elided.

title: Digenis is dying
author: Anonymous (folk song)
intro: Digenis Akritas, 'the border-guard of two races' (son of an Arab emir and a Greek mother), is the hero of a Byzantine epic and of many folk songs about the akrites who defended the eastern frontier of the empire. In this ballad the giant hero lies dying and the whole cosmos trembles. Folk songs live in many variants; these are the opening lines of a widely anthologized version, in the fifteen-syllable 'political verse' of Greek folk poetry, with its typical folk forms (τονε, εσκέπαζε, αϊτός).

tr.en: Digenis is in his death-throes, and the earth is afraid of him.
The sky thunders and flashes, and the upper world shakes,
and the underworld has opened, and its foundations creak,
and the gravestone shudders at how it will cover him,
how it will cover the eagle, the hero of the earth.
No house could roof him, no cave could hold him;
he strode across mountains, leapt from peak to peak,
he tossed boulders like quoits and shifted rooted rocks.

notes.n: Διγενής means 'of two races' (δι- + γένος). ψυχομαχώ 'struggle with one's soul' is the folk word for being in the throes of death (ψυχή + μάχομαι 'fight'). τονε is a lengthened τον, used for the metre. τρομάσσει is an old spelling of τρομάζει, here 'is terrified of'.

βροντά 'thunders' (βροντή 'thunder') and αστράφτει 'lightens' (Ancient ἀστράπτω). σειέτ’ (σειέται with its final vowel elided) 'shakes' is the passive of σείω, the root of σεισμός 'earthquake' and English seismic. ο απάνω κόσμος, the world of the living, is set against ο κάτω κόσμος, the underworld (απάνω = πάνω).
θεμέλια 'foundations' is Ancient θεμέλιον, from τίθημι 'set, place'. τρίζω 'creak, grate' is an Ancient imitative verb.

πλάκα 'slab, gravestone' is Ancient πλάξ, πλακός 'flat stone'; the related πλακοῦς 'flat cake' gave Latin placenta. ανατριχιά is a folk form of ανατριχιάζει 'shudders' — literally 'one's hair (τρίχα) stands up'.

αϊτός is the folk form of αετός 'eagle' (Ancient ἀετός), the stock image of the brave young man in folk songs. αντρειωμένος 'brave, heroic' comes from αντρεία 'valour' (ἀνήρ, ἀνδρός 'man'). τση is the Cretan and Ionian form of the article της.

εσκέπαζε and εχώρει are imperfects with the old augment ε- that folk songs love. σκεπάζω 'cover, roof' is from σκέπη 'shelter'; σπήλιο is a folk form of σπήλαιο 'cave' (speleology); χωρώ 'hold, have room for' is Ancient χωρέω.

όρη is the plural of όρος 'mountain', the Ancient word that everyday speech replaced with βουνό. διασκελίζω 'stride across' comes from σκέλος 'leg' (isosceles 'equal-legged'). βουνού κορφές 'peaks of the mountain(s)': κορφή 'peak' is the folk form of κορυφή. επήδα is an old imperfect of πηδάω 'leap' (modern πηδούσε).

A Cretan line of giant's play. χαράκια (here elided χαράκι’) are huge stones or crags, from Ancient χάραξ; αμαδολόγανε 'he played amades with them' is from αμάδα, a stone thrown like a discus or quoit in a folk game; ριζιμιά are rocks rooted in the ground (ρίζα 'root'), and ξεκούνειε is a dialect imperfect of ξεκουνώ 'dislodge, shift' (standard ξεκουνούσε).

title: Easter in the village
intro: Easter, not Christmas, is the great feast of the Greek year, and many city families return to their village for it. The text follows Holy Week from the dyeing of the eggs to the midnight Resurrection service and the lamb on the spit. The liturgical phrases are in Koine Greek, still sung unchanged in every church.

tr.en: Easter is the greatest feast of the year for the Greeks.
Every year many Athenians leave the city and go back to their village.
In Holy Week the housewives dye eggs red and bake tsourekia.
On the evening of Good Friday the Epitaphios, decked with flowers, passes through the streets.
The whole village follows it with candles in their hands, chanting mournful hymns.
On Holy Saturday, a little before midnight, everyone gathers at the church.
The lights go out and the priest comes out with a lighted candle.
"Come, receive the light," he chants, and the light passes from candle to candle.
At exactly twelve "Christ is risen!" rings out and the bells peal for joy.
People kiss one another and answer: "Truly he is risen!"
Then everyone goes home with the holy light and eats magiritsa.
On Easter Sunday they roast lamb on the spit, dance and make merry until evening.
They also play the egg-cracking game: whoever has the strongest egg wins!

notes.n: Πάσχα comes from Hebrew/Aramaic pesach/pascha 'Passover'. Through Latin pascha it gave Italian Pasqua, Spanish Pascua and French Pâques. It is indeclinable: το Πάσχα, του Πάσχα. γιορτή 'feast' is Ancient ἑορτή.

Holy Week is 'the Great Week' (Μεγάλη Εβδομάδα), and each of its days is 'Great': Μεγάλη Πέμπτη, Μεγάλη Παρασκευή, Μεγάλο Σάββατο. νοικοκυρά 'housewife' goes back to οἰκοκύρης 'master (κύριος) of the house (οἶκος)'. κόκκινος 'red' is from κόκκος 'grain' — the kermes insect, which looks like a grain and gave a red dye. τσουρέκι, the sweet braided Easter bread, is Turkish çörek.

Παρασκευή 'Friday' is Ancient παρασκευή 'preparation' (for the Sabbath). The Επιτάφιος — 'on the tomb', the word behind English epitaph — is the embroidered image of the dead Christ on a flower-decked bier. στολισμένος is the passive participle of στολίζω 'adorn', from στολή 'equipment, dress'.
ψάλλω 'chant' is Ancient ψάλλω 'pluck (a string)', whence ψαλμός, psalm. τροπάριο 'hymn' is a diminutive of τρόπος 'manner, mode'. κερί 'candle' is Ancient κηρίον 'honeycomb', from κηρός 'wax'.
Σάββατο 'Saturday' is Hebrew shabbat, via Greek σάββατον; Latin sabbatum gave Italian sabato and French samedi. μεσάνυχτα 'midnight' is 'mid-night' (μέσος + νύχτα), a plural noun.

παπάς 'priest' is Byzantine παπᾶς 'father' — the same baby-word as Pope. φως 'light' (Ancient φῶς, from φάος) has the irregular plural φώτα. αναμμένο 'lit' is the participle of ανάβω, Ancient ἀνάπτω 'kindle'.
«Δεύτε λάβετε φως» is Byzantine liturgical Greek: δεῦτε 'come (all of you)!' and λάβετε, the aorist imperative of λαμβάνω 'take'. In everyday Greek one would say Ελάτε να πάρετε φως.

Χριστός ανέστη 'Christ is risen'. Χριστός 'anointed' (χρίω 'anoint') translates Hebrew Messiah. ανέστη is the Koine aorist of ἀνίσταμαι 'rise' — Modern Greek says αναστήθηκε; the noun is ανάσταση 'resurrection'. καμπάνα 'bell' is Latin campana, 'the metal of Campania'.

Αληθώς ανέστη 'truly he is risen' — αληθώς is the Ancient adverb of ἀληθής 'true'; today one says αλήθεια or πραγματικά. φιλιούνται 'kiss each other': the passive form of a verb often expresses a reciprocal action.
μαγειρίτσα is a soup of lamb offal and herbs that breaks the forty-day fast after the midnight service; the name comes from μαγειρεύω 'cook'.

αρνί 'lamb' is Ancient ἀρνίον, a diminutive of ἀρήν. Many everyday Modern Greek nouns continue such diminutives: αρνί, πουλί 'bird' (πουλίον), ψάρι 'fish' (ὀψάριον). σούβλα 'spit' is Latin subula 'awl'.
τσούγκρισμα comes from τσουγκρίζω 'knock together', an imitative word. γερός 'strong, sound' is Ancient ὑγιηρός 'healthy', with its first syllable lost.

title: The Lord's Prayer
author: Gospel of Matthew
source: Matthew 6:9–13, as recited in the Greek Orthodox Church
intro: The Lord's Prayer in the Koine Greek of the New Testament, recited unchanged in every Greek Orthodox church and by many Greeks every day. Every Greek understands it, yet almost every form in it differs from Modern Greek: the dative case, third-person imperatives, ancient pronouns and verb forms. Church books print it in polytonic script; here it is given in monotonic like the rest of this collection, and the notes show how each line would be said today.

tr.en: Our Father, who are in heaven,
hallowed be your name,
your kingdom come,
your will be done,
as in heaven, so also on earth.
Give us today our daily bread,
and forgive us our debts,
as we too forgive our debtors.
And do not lead us into temptation,
but deliver us from the evil one.
Amen.

notes.n: Πάτερ is the Ancient vocative of πατήρ; Modern Greek says Πατέρα, from the new nominative πατέρας built on the old accusative πατέρα. ημών 'of us, our' is today μας. ο εν τοις ουρανοίς 'who (are) in the heavens' uses εν + dative, a case lost in the spoken language; today: που είσαι στους ουρανούς.

αγιασθήτω 'let it be hallowed' is a third-person imperative, a form Modern Greek has lost; the modern language uses ας + subjunctive: ας αγιαστεί το όνομά σου. αγιάζω comes from άγιος 'holy' (hagiography).
ελθέτω 'let it come' — modern ας έρθει. βασιλεία 'kingdom' is from βασιλεύς 'king', the family of basilica and the name Basil.
γενηθήτω 'let it be done' is the Koine passive aorist of γίνομαι 'become, happen' — modern ας γίνει. θέλημα 'will' is from θέλω 'want'.
ως … και 'as … so also'. εν ουρανώ 'in heaven' is a dative; επί της γης 'upon the earth' is ἐπί with the genitive. Today one would say όπως στον ουρανό, έτσι και στη γη.

άρτος is the Ancient word for bread, kept in church language; everyday Greek says ψωμί, but άρτος lives on in αρτοποιείο 'bakery'. επιούσιος is a rare word found almost only here; it may mean 'for the coming day' or 'needed for our existence' (Latin quotīdiānus, or Jerome's supersubstantiālis). δος 'give!' is the Ancient imperative of δίδωμι (modern δώσε); ημίν 'to us' is a dative (modern μας); σήμερον keeps the ancient final -ν of σήμερα.

άφες 'let go, forgive' is the aorist imperative of ἀφίημι, whose aorist ἀφῆκα gave Modern αφήνω 'let, leave'; 'forgive' is now συγχωρώ. οφειλήματα 'debts' comes from οφείλω 'owe', still used in formal Greek.

ημείς is the Ancient form of εμείς 'we', whose first vowel changed under the influence of εγώ. αφίεμεν 'we forgive' would be συγχωρούμε today. οφειλέταις is the dative plural of οφειλέτης 'debtor', a word still in everyday legal use.

εισενέγκης is the aorist subjunctive of εἰσφέρω 'bring in', with the irregular aorist stem ἐνεγκ-; μη + aorist subjunctive is the Ancient way of forbidding. εις 'into' is the ancestor of Modern σε. πειρασμός 'temptation' comes from πειράζω 'test', which in Modern Greek means 'tease, bother'. In modern words: μη μας φέρεις σε πειρασμό.

ρύσαι 'rescue!' is the aorist imperative of ῥύομαι, a verb unknown to Modern Greek, which would say γλίτωσέ μας or σώσε μας. του πονηρού can mean 'the evil one' or 'evil'. πονηρός meant 'wicked' in Ancient Greek; today it means 'sly, cunning'.
αμήν is Hebrew 'truly, so be it', taken into Greek and Latin with the Bible.

title: Hymn to Liberty
author: Dionysios Solomos
intro: Dionysios Solomos (1798–1857), from Zakynthos, wrote the 158 stanzas of the "Hymn to Liberty" in May 1823, in the middle of the Greek War of Independence. Set to music by Nikolaos Mantzaros, its opening stanzas became the national anthem of Greece (and of Cyprus). Solomos wrote in the spoken language of the Ionian Islands rather than in learned Greek, but his demotic contains older and local forms (εκατοικούσες, ακαρτερούσες, άργειε) that are explained in the notes. The title itself is katharevousa.

tr.en: I know you by the edge
of your terrible sword,
I know you by the look
that measures out the earth with force.
Sprung from the sacred bones
of the Greeks,
and valiant as you were of old,
hail, O hail, Liberty!
There inside you dwelt,
embittered, full of shame,
and you waited for a voice
to say to you, "Come again."
That day was slow to come,
and everything was silent,
for fear overshadowed it all
and slavery weighed it down.

notes.n: κόψη 'cutting edge' is from κόβω 'cut' (Ancient κόπτω). σπαθί 'sword' is Byzantine σπαθίον, from σπάθη 'broad blade', which Latin borrowed as spatha — hence Italian spada, Spanish espada, French épée.
όψη 'look, face' is Ancient ὄψις 'sight' (optics, synopsis).
βία 'force' is read as one syllable (βια) for the metre. Some readers take με βία as 'in haste'. μετράει is the colloquial form of μετρά 'measures' (μετράω, Ancient μετρέω).

βγαλμένη 'brought out, risen' is the participle of βγάζω 'take out', the causative partner of βγαίνω 'go out' (Ancient ἐκβαίνω). The idea: Liberty rises from the bones of the ancient and fallen Greeks.
Note the poetic word order: των Ελλήνων τα ιερά (κόκαλα) 'the sacred (bones) of the Greeks'. ιερός 'holy' is Ancient ἱερός (hierarchy, hieroglyph).
σαν πρώτα 'as before, as of old'. ανδρειωμένη 'valiant' (also αντρειωμένη) comes from ανδρεία 'courage', Ancient ἀνδρεία 'manliness' (ἀνήρ, ἀνδρός 'man').

χαίρε is the Ancient imperative χαῖρε 'rejoice!', the Greek greeting — the same word the angel says to Mary (χαῖρε, κεχαριτωμένη), Latin avē. Ελευθεριά is ελευθερία with the stress moved to the end, as in the popular form λευτεριά; ἐλεύθερος 'free' is Ancient.
εκατοικούσες 'you were dwelling' keeps an old syllabic augment ε-, as the Ionian dialect did; Modern Greek says κατοικούσες. κατοικώ is Ancient κατοικέω (οἶκος 'house').
εντροπαλή is the older form of ντροπαλή 'bashful, ashamed', from ντροπή 'shame', Ancient ἐντροπή 'turning inward'. πικραμένη 'embittered' is from πικρός 'bitter'.
ακαρτερούσες 'you were waiting' is καρτερούσες with a prothetic α-, a common feature of folk and Ionian speech. καρτερώ is Ancient καρτερέω 'endure, hold out'.
έλα 'come!' is the imperative of έρχομαι. The 'mouth' is a voice from abroad, an ally who would call Greece to rise again.

Άργειε is an Ionian imperfect of αργώ 'be late, be slow' (standard αργούσε). νά ’λθει is να έλθει (modern να έρθει), 'to come', with the initial vowel dropped; the accent on νά shows that the stress now falls there.

τα ’σκιαζε is τα έσκιαζε 'overshadowed them, terrified them' with the initial vowel dropped (the stress falls on τα). σκιάζω comes from σκιά 'shadow'; φοβέρα 'threat, terror' from φόβος 'fear' (phobia).
σκλαβιά 'slavery' comes from σκλάβος 'slave', Byzantine σκλάβος 'a Slav' (Medieval Latin sclavus) — the same history as English slave. πλακώνω 'crush, press down' is from πλάκα 'slab'.

title: Ithaca
author: C. P. Cavafy
intro: Constantine P. Cavafy (1863–1933), the Greek poet of Alexandria, published "Ithaca" in 1911. Taking Odysseus' long voyage home as its image, the poem argues that the journey, not the arrival, is the reward. Cavafy's language blends everyday demotic with learned katharevousa forms (σκέψις, φθάσιμον), and his spelling has quirks of its own (νάναι, η Ιθάκες), which are kept here.

tr.en: As you set out on the journey to Ithaca,
pray that the road be long,
full of adventures, full of knowledge.
The Laestrygonians and the Cyclopes,
angry Poseidon — do not be afraid of them;
you will never find such things on your way
if your thought stays lofty, if a rare
emotion touches your spirit and your body.
The Laestrygonians and the Cyclopes,
savage Poseidon you will not meet,
unless you carry them within your soul,
unless your soul sets them up before you.
Pray that the road be long.
May there be many summer mornings
when — with what pleasure, with what joy —
you will enter harbours seen for the first time;
may you stop at Phoenician trading posts
and acquire the fine wares,
mother-of-pearl and coral, amber and ebony,
and sensual perfumes of every kind,
as many sensual perfumes as you can;
may you go to many Egyptian cities,
to learn and learn again from the learned.
Always keep Ithaca in your mind.
To arrive there is your destination.
But do not hurry the journey at all.
Better that it last many years,
and that you anchor at the island an old man at last,
rich with all you have gained on the way,
not expecting Ithaca to give you riches.
Ithaca gave you the beautiful journey.
Without her you would never have set out.
She has nothing more to give you.
And if you find her poor, Ithaca has not deceived you.
Wise as you have become, with so much experience,

w: nom. pl. f. (Cavafy's spelling of οι)

tr.en: you will have understood by now what Ithacas mean.

notes.n: Σα (= σαν) here means 'when, as soon as'. πηγαιμός 'going, outward journey' is a folk-song word, from πηγαίνω. Ιθάκη is Odysseus' island home, the goal of the Odyssey.
νάναι is Cavafy's fused spelling of να είναι (standard να 'ναι); likewise νάχεις (line 24) and θάβγαινες (line 32). εύχομαι 'wish, pray' is Ancient εὔχομαι.

Λαιστρυγόνας and Κύκλωπας are Ancient accusative plurals (Modern Greek would say τους Λαιστρυγόνες, τους Κύκλωπες). The man-eating Laestrygonians appear in Odyssey 10, the Cyclopes in Odyssey 9; Κύκλωψ means 'round-eye' (κύκλος + ὤψ).

σκέψις, συγκίνησις (line 8) and ευχαρίστησι (line 15) keep the katharevousa ending -ις/-ι of Ancient -σις (Latin -sis); spoken Greek says σκέψη, συγκίνηση, ευχαρίστηση. μέν’ is μένει with its last vowel elided. υψηλή 'lofty' is the learned form of everyday ψηλή.
κουβανείς is a variant of κουβαλάς 'you carry'. μες is a shortened μέσα 'inside'.
πρωιά 'mornings', the plural of πρωί (Ancient πρωΐ 'early').

λιμένας is the learned form of 'harbour' (Ancient λιμήν); the everyday word is λιμάνι. πρωτοειδωμένους 'seen for the first time' is Cavafy's own compound of πρώτο and ειδωμένος, the participle of βλέπω (aorist passive ειδώθηκα).
The Phoenicians were the great merchants of the ancient Mediterranean. εμπορείο 'trading post' is Ancient ἐμπόριον, which Latin borrowed as emporium.
τες is an older and dialectal form of the article τις, common in Cavafy. πραγμάτεια 'merchandise' comes from πράγμα 'thing'.

The list mixes origins: σεντέφι 'mother-of-pearl' is Turkish sedef and κεχριμπάρι 'amber' is Turkish kehribar (from Persian), while κοράλλι is Ancient κοράλλιον (Latin corallium, English coral) and έβενος is Ancient ἔβενος, from Egyptian, which gave Latin ebenus and English ebony.
ηδονικός 'sensual' is from ηδονή 'pleasure' (hedonism). μυρωδικά 'perfumes, spices' comes from μύρον 'scented oil'. κάθε λογής 'of every kind' uses the genitive of λογή 'sort'.
σπουδασμένοι 'the learned' is the participle of σπουδάζω 'study'. The repeated να μάθεις stresses that the learning never ends.
νους 'mind' is Ancient νοῦς (Attic contraction of νόος), as in English 'use your nous'.
φθάσιμον 'arriving' is a demotic verbal noun (φτάσιμο) dressed in katharevousa clothes, with learned φθ and an ancient final -ν. είν’ is είναι with its last vowel elided.
Καλλίτερα is the old spelling of καλύτερα 'better', once written with -λλ- by association with κάλλος 'beauty'.
αράζω 'cast anchor, moor' is a sailors' word; in today's slang it also means 'chill out'.

προσδοκώντας 'expecting' is a demotic gerund formed on a learned verb (Ancient προσδοκάω). σε δώσει 'give you' uses the accusative of the indirect object, as in Constantinople and northern Greece; standard Greek says σου δώσει.
πτωχικός 'poor, humble' is learned (Ancient πτωχός 'beggar'); everyday Greek says φτωχικός. γελάω 'laugh' also means 'fool, deceive': η Ιθάκη δεν σε γέλασε.

θα + aorist expresses a probable past: θα το κατάλαβες 'you must have understood'. η Ιθάκες shows Cavafy's habit of writing the feminine plural article οι as η — the two have been pronounced alike for centuries.

title: Olympic Hymn
author: Kostis Palamas
intro: Kostis Palamas (1859–1943), the leading Greek poet of his generation, wrote this hymn for the first modern Olympic Games, held in Athens in 1896, and Spyridon Samaras set it to music. In 1958 the International Olympic Committee made it the official Olympic anthem, sung in Greek at the opening of every Games. The poem invokes the ancient spirit of Greece to come down and bless the contests.

tr.en: Ancient Spirit, immortal, pure father
of the beautiful, the great and the true,
come down, reveal yourself and flash like lightning here
in the glory of your own earth and sky.

notes.n: A string of vocatives. Neuters have the same form in all three direct cases (Αρχαίο Πνεύμ’ αθάνατον — Πνεύμ’ is πνεύμα with its final vowel elided, and αθάνατον keeps the old final -ν), masculines in -ος take -ε (αγνός → αγνέ), and πατέρας drops its -ς (πατέρα). πνεύμα is Ancient πνεῦμα 'breath, wind, spirit' (pneumatic, pneumonia); αθάνατος 'immortal' is ἀ- + θάνατος 'death'.

'The beautiful, the great and the true': neuter adjectives with the article serve as abstract nouns, as in Plato's τὸ καλόν and τὸ ἀληθές. τ’ is του with its vowel elided. ωραίος 'beautiful' is Ancient ὡραῖος 'in season, ripe' (ὥρα 'season, hour').

κατέβα 'come down!' is the imperative of κατεβαίνω (Ancient καταβαίνω). φανερώσου 'show yourself' is the passive imperative of φανερώνω, from φανερός 'visible' (the root of phenomenon). άστραψ’ (άστραψε, elided before εδώ) 'flash!' is from αστράφτω, Ancient ἀστράπτω, whence αστραπή 'lightning'. εδώ πέρα is a colloquial 'right here'.
δόξα 'glory' is Ancient δόξα 'opinion, reputation' — compare doxology and orthodox 'of right opinion'. γης is the genitive of γη 'earth'; ουρανός 'sky, heaven' is Ancient οὐρανός, the god Uranus.

title: The City
author: C. P. Cavafy
intro: "The City" (1910) opens Cavafy's collected poems. In the first stanza a man in quotation marks dreams of escaping to another land and another sea; in the second the poet answers him that the city — his own life — will follow him wherever he goes. It is one of Cavafy's few rhymed poems: each stanza ends on the rhyme it began with (θάλασσα – χάλασα, θάλασσες – χάλασες).

tr.en: You said: "I will go to another land, I will go to another sea.
Another city will be found, better than this one.
Every effort of mine is a sentence already written;
and my heart lies buried, like a corpse.
How long will my mind remain in this decay?
Wherever I turn my eye, wherever I look,
I see the black ruins of my life here,
where I spent so many years, and wrecked and wasted them."
You will find no new lands, you will find no other seas.
The city will follow you. You will roam the same

w: σε + art. acc. pl. f. (old form)

tr.en: streets. And in the same neighbourhoods you will grow old;
and in these same houses you will turn grey.
You will always arrive in this city. Do not hope for elsewhere —
there is no ship for you, there is no road.
As you have wrecked your life here,
in this small corner, you have ruined it in the whole world.

notes.n: πάγω is the older form of πάω 'go', itself worn down from Ancient ὑπάγω. γη 'earth, land' is Ancient γῆ (geography, geology). The raised dot after Είπες is the Greek ano teleia, used like a colon or semicolon.
πόλις is the Ancient (and katharevousa) nominative; spoken Greek says πόλη. Compare English politics and metropolis. καλλίτερη is an old spelling of καλύτερη 'better'.
καταδίκη 'condemnation, sentence' is κατά + δίκη 'justice, lawsuit'. γραφτή 'written' — i.e. fated in advance.
θαμμένη 'buried' is the participle of θάβω, Ancient θάπτω — the root of τάφος 'tomb' and English epitaph.

μαρασμόν keeps the final -ν of the Ancient accusative. μαρασμός 'wasting away' comes from μαραίνω 'wither' (medical marasmus). Like the last line of 'Waiting for the Barbarians', this question ends with a full stop.
ερείπια 'ruins' is Ancient ἐρείπια, from ἐρείπω 'throw down'.

ρημάζω 'lay waste' comes from έρημος 'deserted' (ἐρημίτης, English hermit). χαλώ 'ruin, spoil' is Ancient χαλάω 'loosen'. The closing quotation mark ends the speaker's words; the second stanza is the poet's answer.
θάβρεις is Cavafy's fused spelling of θα βρεις. καινούριος (standard καινούργιος) is Byzantine καινουργής 'newly made' (καινός 'new' + ἔργον 'work').
στες and τες are older forms of στις, τις. γερνάω 'grow old' is from γέρος 'old man', Ancient γέρων (gerontology).
ασπρίζω 'turn white' comes from άσπρος 'white', which goes back to Latin asper 'rough' — the word for freshly minted, bright silver coins.
τα αλλού 'the elsewheres': an adverb turned into a noun with the article. πόλι is the learned accusative without its final -ν.

δεν έχει 'there is no' — impersonal έχει 'there is', just like Spanish hay (from Latin habet) and French il y a. οδός 'road' is Ancient ὁδός, feminine, as in exodus and method (μέθοδος 'the way after').
κώχη 'nook, corner' is a colloquial word; τούτος 'this' continues Ancient οὗτος. The final line rhymes with the first line of the stanza: θάλασσες – χάλασες.

title: Waiting for the Barbarians
author: C. P. Cavafy
intro: Cavafy's most famous poem, written in 1898 and printed in 1904. In an unnamed city of the late Roman Empire one voice asks why the Senate, the emperor and the consuls are all waiting in their finery; another answers that the barbarians are coming. The Roman setting fills the poem with Latin institutions in Greek dress — Σύγκλητος, ύπατοι, πραίτορες, τόγες — and Cavafy mixes katharevousa (αυτοκράτωρ, πόλεως, σύγχυσις) with demotic.

tr.en: — What are we waiting for, gathered in the forum?
The barbarians are to arrive today.
— Why such inaction in the Senate?
Why do the Senators sit there and make no laws?
Because the barbarians will arrive today.
What laws should the Senators make now?
When the barbarians come, they will make the laws.
— Why has our emperor risen so early,
and sits at the city's greatest gate,
upon the throne, in state, wearing the crown?
Because the barbarians will arrive today.
And the emperor is waiting to receive
their leader. He has even prepared
a parchment to give him. On it
he has written many titles and names for him.
— Why have our two consuls and the praetors come out
today in their red, embroidered togas;
why have they put on bracelets with so many amethysts,
and rings with brilliant, glittering emeralds;
why should they carry precious canes today,
finely worked in silver and gold?
Because the barbarians will arrive today;
and things like these dazzle the barbarians.
— Why don't our worthy orators come as usual
to deliver their speeches, to have their say?
Because the barbarians will arrive today;
and they are bored by eloquence and harangues.
— Why should this unease suddenly begin,
and this confusion? (How grave the faces have become!)
Why are the streets and squares emptying so fast,
and everyone going home so lost in thought?
Because night has fallen and the barbarians have not come.
And some men have arrived from the frontier
and said that there are no barbarians any longer.
And now, what is to become of us without barbarians.
Those people were a kind of solution.

notes.n: The poem is a dialogue: the lines opened by a dash are the questions, the others the replies (indented in printed editions). αγορά is the Greek for the Roman forum. συναθροισμένοι 'assembled' is a learned participle (συν + ἀθροίζω 'gather').
Είναι ... να φθάσουν 'they are to arrive'. φθάνω is the learned spelling of φτάνω: spoken Greek turned φθ, χθ into φτ, χτ (χθες → χτες), but Cavafy keeps the older spelling.
Σύγκλητος 'Senate' is the Greek name of the Roman Senate: (ἡ) σύγκλητος (βουλή) 'the council called together' (συγκαλέω) — feminine like βουλή. Today it is the senate of a university.
Τι 'why?' (literally 'what?'). κάθοντ’ is κάθονται with the final vowel elided; νομοθετούνε has the extended ending -ούνε, common in poetry and speech.
κάμουν is the older form of κάνουν (aorist έκαμα). νόμος 'law' is Ancient νόμος (astronomy, economy).
αυτοκράτωρ is the katharevousa nominative (Modern αυτοκράτορας), the Greek rendering of Latin imperator: 'self-ruler'. σηκώθη is a shortened older form of σηκώθηκε 'he got up'.
πόλεως is the Ancient genitive of πόλις (Modern πόλης); the poet places it inside the phrase στης πόλεως την πιο μεγάλη πύλη 'at the city's greatest gate'.
κορώνα 'crown' is a round trip: Ancient κορώνη 'anything curved' became Latin corōna, which came back as Italian corona → κορώνα. φορώντας 'wearing' is the gerund of φορώ.
περγαμηνή 'parchment' is named after Pergamon in Asia Minor, where it was perfected — Latin pergamēna, French parchemin, English parchment.
ύπατος 'highest' was the Greek word for a Roman consul; πραίτορες is Latin praetores. εβγήκαν keeps the syllabic augment ε- of Ancient verbs (Modern βγήκαν).
τόγα is Latin toga. τες is the older form of the article τις. κεντημένες 'embroidered' is from κεντώ 'prick, embroider' (Ancient κεντέω — the root of κέντρον 'point, centre').

βραχιόλι 'bracelet' is from βραχίων 'arm', which went into Latin as bracchium (Italian braccio, French bras, English bracelet). αμέθυστος is 'not drunk' (ἀ- + μεθύω): the stone was believed to prevent drunkenness.
σμαράγδι 'emerald' is Ancient σμάραγδος, Latin smaragdus, which became English emerald. δαχτυλίδι 'ring' is from δάχτυλο 'finger' (Ancient δάκτυλος, cf. dactyl).
μπαστούνι 'stick, cane' is Italian bastone.
ασήμι 'silver' is Ancient ἄσημον 'unmarked', i.e. uncoined silver bullion. μάλαμα 'gold' is a folk word from μάλαγμα 'something softened', soft gold. σκαλίζω 'carve, engrave'.
ρήτορας 'orator' is Ancient ῥήτωρ (rhetoric). άξιος 'worthy' is Ancient ἄξιος (axiom).
βαριέμαι 'be bored' comes from βαρύς 'heavy'. ευφράδεια 'eloquence' and δημηγορία 'public speech' (δῆμος + ἀγορεύω, cf. demagogue) are learned words.
μονομιάς 'all at once' is 'at one go' (μονο- + μιας, the genitive of μία).
εγίναν is Cavafy's stress for έγιναν 'became', placing the accent where the iambic metre needs it.
πλατέες is Cavafy's spelling of πλατείες 'squares'. πλατεία 'square' is Ancient πλατεῖα (ὁδός) 'broad (street)', which through Latin platea became Italian piazza, Spanish plaza, French place.
ενύχτωσε 'night fell', with the old augment ε-; from νύχτα 'night', Ancient νύξ, νυκτός.
γένουμε is the older form of γίνουμε. Cavafy ends the question with a full stop, not a question mark.
ήσαν is the older form of ήταν 'they were'; λύσις is the learned form of λύση 'solution' (Ancient λύσις 'loosening'; cf. analysis).
